articles.content: The fourth of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. There is no crisis experience promised or commanded as an essential element in living the Christian life. Some teaching on the Christian life asserts that only a low level of Christian experience can be realized by the person who has not had a crisis experience subsequent to regeneration, or at least subsequent to conversion and to the beginning of conscious Christian experience. Furthermore, it is asserted that the crisis experience is both commanded and promised by God as the entrance into a qualitatively new dimension or level of spiritual experience, reality and power. Throughout the history of the Christian church there have been many different strands of this crisis teaching. There is what we might call ‘classic Wesleyan perfectionism,’ which concentrated particularly upon sanctification and spoke of a baptism of purifying fire, or of coming into a state of perfect love. It concentrated not so much on power for service or upon inward feelings, but on a crisis experience in which the power of indwelling sin was to all intents and purposes negated. I have read enough of classic Wesleyan theology to know that there are different opinions as to what John Wesley himself taught on the subject. But in a general descriptive manner this, I believe, is an accurate representation of old-style classic Wesleyan perfectionism. Then, too, there is ‘the old Pentecostalism’ in which the emphasis was upon a baptism in the Holy Spirit, generally subsequent to conversion, and invariably manifested by speaking in tongues: the way you knew that you had this baptism of power was that, when it came to you, you spoke in tongues. The primary focus in old classic Pentecostalism was the matter of power for service. Thirdly, there is the modern ‘charismatic movement.’ Like classic Pentecostalism, its teachers use many of the same passages in the Book of Acts to support their theory of this necessary crisis. So they emphasize that in most cases—although there are different schools among modern charismatics—it will be manifested by the speaking in tongues. Some are content to believe you have ‘got it’ if you have a season of holy laughter. Others, however, say that you have not spoken in tongues because you have some psychological hold-ups, and if these can be removed the tongues are there. You just have not given them utterance. Here the emphasis is not so much on a baptism of purifying fire (as in the case of old classic Wesleyan perfectionism), or the baptism of power (as in the case of old classic Pentecostalism), but more upon a baptism of joyful praise-filled experience. I have been speaking of generalities, but I believe they are accurate. Fourthly, there are the various forms of ‘higher life’ teaching. What they have in common is this: you are simply converted, simply united to Christ, simply regenerated, and then you come to a crisis of surrender and faith, in which ‘you let go and let God’ and appropriate the indwelling life of Christ. The common denominator is that it is a crisis without any external manifestation of tongues or holy laughter or shouting or jumping, but the end result will be new power to live a holy life—the emphasis falls upon the ability to be more efficient in the path of holiness. Fifthly, there is a kind of teaching which has both old and modern proponents. It focuses on assurance, and has been expressed in terms of the biblical language of a ‘sealing of the Holy Spirit.’ Some of the Puritans—Thomas Goodwin, for example—taught this. There have been certain preachers in our own day who have believed this very strongly and emphasized it repeatedly. The basic concern in this teaching is that, subsequent to regeneration and conversion, there is a crisis experience in which the believer enters into a qualitatively new dimension of assurance by

articles.content: Iain H. Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes is a short retelling of the remarkable life of the Irish missionary to India. What follows is Chapter 4 of that title, ‘Hard Days and Golden Years.’ If there was any pattern to Amy Carmichael’s life it was of times of refreshing then of trials, of exhilarating ‘climbing’ then of walking in dark ravines. In part her explanation was that demonic activity follows the work of the Holy Spirit. As she quoted from George Bowen, When Christianity assumes an aggressive attitude the first result is a great exhibition of Satanic power. Satan’s power to be manifested must be assaulted. 1 Such an understanding does not come so readily to us who do not live, as she did, within sight of demon possession, or within hearing of tom-tom drums calling devotees to idols. Shortly before Walker 2 had left on his last mission, he had been sitting with Amy and others in deck chairs under the stars. ‘We had been talking’, she later wrote, of work and workers, and of those (to me) most wonderful women, who seemed perfectly self-reliant, needing no strong arm alongside. I remember how, suddenly startled at the bare thought of working alone, in the sense of all the burden of responsibility, I exclaimed that I never could do it. Mr Walker laughed. ‘Well, you don’t have to’, he said. 3 Amy was the weaker when her ‘strong arm’ died at the age of fifty-four. What she owed to Walker’s ‘courageous championship’ of the children’s work, ‘through its first very difficult years, no words can tell, nor can words tell how he is missed’. 4 At times, as she faced her loss, she would need to say to herself, ‘Don’t give up, don’t be afraid: go on.’ Prayer for ‘fortitude’ entered her life. There were unsympathetic neighbours who observed the work at Dohnavur who supposed that Amy would now be more vulnerable. One of these was a lawyer who, soon after Walker’s death, wrote with the demand that current work on the building of a wall around the compoundbe stopped, and that a half-built nursery should be pulled down. They were using ground, he claimed, to which they did not have legal title. ‘He had waited till Mr Walker’s death had left us, as he thought, defenceless, almost desolate, and sure to be easily cowed by threats of court trouble.’ The wall building had been prompted by the passage of a tiger through the compound at night; and the new nursery was necessitated by the growing numbers of children for whom Dohnavur had become home. Amy ignored the letter and heard nothing more of the threat. The Dohnavur family of seventy children and grown-ups in 1906, had doubled itself by this date, and the need of more helpers was pressing. Mrs Catherine Carmichael was never able to return. She died on July 14, 1913. A few weeks earlier a letter from her to Amy began with the words, ‘My own most precious earthly possession’. While Amy did not lament her mother’s death—for no Christian death was to be ‘lamented’—in the days ahead she needed to preach to herself, ‘I must remind myself to live in the joy of those gone, not grovel in the sense of my loss.’ Mrs Carmichael had been a constant supporter and representative for Dohnavur in Britain. She acted as the home secretary to whom gifts could be sent, and helped to make her daughter’s books more widely known. In 1912 those books had been noted by Queen Mary, wife of King George V, who expressed her thanks for them. While Amy was busy in 1913 writing Walker of Tinnevelly , there came the possibility of the loss of her closest female friend and helper, Ponnammal, who had been with her ever since, as a young widow, she had come to new life through Walker’s preaching. She now needed surgery for cancer and Amy went with her to a Salvation Army Hospital at Neyyoor for a period. In their absence from Dohnavur (forty-six miles away), and the absence of Mabel Wade who was on furlough, 70 of the children were ill. articles.content: The second of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. Principle 2: There is no escape from tension and conflict in living the Christian life. I do not say that the Christian life is all tension and all conflict. The kind of teaching I am attempting to expose as fallacious is as follows: At a conference a speaker takes a text out of context to which he attaches or from which he extracts a shibboleth – perhaps the shibboleth of Christ living his life through us, or the saving life of Christ, or the abiding life. Then the preacher, having expounded his theory of the Christian life, gives an appeal like this: ‘Child of God, are you weary of the tension of wrestling with your remaining sin? Are you tired of struggling in prayer? Are you weary of having to battle with impure thoughts and thoughts of envy and pride and jealousy? Are you tired of this incessant conflict?’ And every true Christian sits there with his fangs dripping, saying, ‘Oh God, you know I am tired, I would give anything to have one day, one day in which I did not have to battle with dullness of heart and distraction of mind and the seductions to sin that come from without and from within’. And the speaker then says ‘Ah, if you are tired of the tension, weary of the conflict, if you will but take these steps, then Christ will so live his life through you that it will be a life marked by the negation of tension and conflict. You will be so filled with the Spirit, so taken up in the Spirit, that tension and conflict for all intents and purposes will be a thing of the past as long as you maintain the posture of the abiding life. The moment you feel tension and conflict, it is because you slipped out of that life, back to your old ways.’ Now that is not a caricature, that is spelled out in page after page, book after book. Beware of the writings of Watchman Nee! Beware of some of the writings of such as Norman Grubb and Hannah Whithall Smith. Beware of these writings, because if you take them seriously they could drive you either into a world of unreality or into a world of scepticism. Now what proof do I offer from the word of God for that proposition? 1. Because of the reality of indwelling sin with its incessant and powerful actions upon us. Galatians 5:17: ‘The flesh is lusting against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh and these two are contrary the one to the other, so that you may not do the things that you would’. And Paul does not go on to say that there is a way to be utterly, totally delivered from that conscious­ness of tension and conflict. He does tell us that we need not be dominated by the flesh: ‘Walk in the Spirit and you shall not fulfil the lusts of the flesh’. But he nowhere says that the consciousness of the flesh’s lusting will be negated, and where flesh is lusting against Spirit, there is conflict. articles.title_zh: 在基督徒的生活中，没有“万能钥匙”
articles.content: The first of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. A question of major importance is ‘How am I to live as a Christian’? It is one thing to be certain on biblical grounds that I have life from Christ, now I must be clear as to how I am to live the life of Christ. My purpose in setting before you some of the major principles of living the Christian life is three-fold: —I wish to sketch in a biblical theology of the Christian life. My purpose is unashamedly one of indoctrination. I wish by God’s help, by Spirit and word, to indoctrinate you in a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. —I wish to inoculate you and to immunize you against the major false views of the Christian life. Some of us desperately wish we had received such an inoculation early in our Christian experience. We spent many years chasing rabbits that we could never catch. We went after experiences and states of mind and heart in the hope that somehow in so doing we would find what it really meant to live as a Christian. —I wish to purge you of any existing misconceptions which you may presently have. It may not be pleasant but it is in your own best interests. We now examine these major principles of the Christian life. Principle 1: There is No One ‘Master Key’ to Living the Christian Life The kind of teaching I am purposing to focus upon in this principle goes something like this: There is a Christian who for many years has found himself in the doldrums. He has had his sails hoisted but he goes nowhere. It seems that he knows little of the wind of the Spirit filling his sails and carrying him anywhere. Or, to change the analogy, he may have his sails hoisted but they seem for ever to be full of holes, and while all around him have hoisted sails and appear to be making progress he seems to be going nowhere. And then one day at a conference or while reading a book or in his own devotions he comes across a passage of Scripture, say John chapter 15, and there he reads in the words of our Lord Jesus that beautiful analogy of the Christian’s relationship to Christ as the relationship of a branch to a vine. This so ignites his own spiritual life that he is almost overnight lifted to an entirely new plateau of spiritual vitality. Either the holes in his sails get mended or it is as though a mighty zephyr from God himself fills his sails, causing them to billow out to the full. He makes more substantial progress in the Christian life in six months than he has made in the previous six years. This man says that the master key to the Christian life is understanding John 15 and if others will only come to understand the concept of Christ’s relationship to his people as the branch and the vine are related they too will come to an entirely new plateau of spiritual vitality and reality in their Christian walk. Another example could be someone who has been struggling with a certain besetting sin which leaves him continually bowed down and crippled with guilt. Here is a young Christian struggling with a certain area of besetting sin, unknown to others, and he is constantly bogged down. His wheels are up to the hub-caps in mud, and no matter how much he changes the gears and pushes down on the accelerator he is spinning his wheels and all he is doing is using up petrol and making a mess. He is in that position for weeks and months perhaps, and then one day at a conference or reading a book or in his own devotions he comes to Romans, chapter 6, and he reads the glorious truth that in union with Jesus Christ all that he was as old man has been put to death, and in union with Jesus Christ the totality of the old life has been buried in Christ’s tomb and he is now a new man in Jesus Christ and he sees that he is called upon to reckon it so, and in the light of that, present himself as alive from the dead. At a listening party in Atlanta on Oct. 12, according to Hot 100.9, Franklin said, “I’ve never done a double album before.” He described the TobyMac collaboration “It Gets Better” as “my attempt to find a space to talk about mental health,” and added, “I’ve had my own journey with anxiety and depression.” He also talked about changes in the Black church. “The Black church culture changed,” he said. “The church got rid of their choirs and the music was in a space that was not my strength.” He had advice for emerging artists, too. “Start off very true and build your audience slow,” he said. “Don’t ride the trends because you don’t know when they’re coming.”

articles.content: San Antonio Spurs rookie Tarris Reed Jr. got baptized days after making his NBA debut, and he posted the video to Instagram under two words: “Jesus Saves.” Reed, a 23-year-old center, was the No. 26 pick in this year’s draft out of UConn. Denver took him, and San Antonio acquired him in a trade. He debuted on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in a 116-104 loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder. In the caption, Reed wrote that he got home late after his first NBA back-to-back and “got my first real glimpse of just how grueling the 82-game NBA season can be.” On the plane ride, he remembered it was Baptism Sunday at his church. “I texted Pastor Ed, and the rest was history LOL.” “It’s been on my heart for a while now to be baptized,” Reed wrote. “I wanted to publicly signify my union with Christ and what it means to walk in His grace, mercy, and NEWNESS OF LIFE!” He quoted Romans 6:4: “We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.” He also wrote about what he sees coming next. “The Lord has placed me in a unique position to help others come to know Christ and experience His life changing power,” he wrote. “To think that I went from wanting nothing to do with the Lord to now desiring to live for Him is something I never could have imagined. I never would have thought my life would look like this.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by TRJ (@iamtarrisreed) Reed is a St. Louis native who started his college career at Michigan, transferred to UConn after his sophomore year and was the Big East Sixth Man of the Year as a junior. In April, UConn lost the national title game to Michigan, and Reed went to Instagram afterward. “I’ve been wrestling with God about this all day” , he wrote in a post that week. “Losing the biggest game of my entire basketball career hurts,” he said. “I tend to be a perfectionist, but only Jesus was perfect.” He wrote that he felt Jesus put it on his heart to go to an Athletes in Action meeting and speak, even though he didn’t want to. He barely had time to prepare, so he told himself he would let the Holy Spirit speak through him. “That night, two of the women’s basketball players got baptized,” he wrote. “It’s not my will, it’s His.” His October post ended with “All glory to God!”

articles.title_zh: 卡尔和劳拉·伦茨谈论五年的公开判断： “你不能从我们的故事中看不到上帝”
articles.content: Five years ago, Laura Lentz had more advice than she wanted. People who had never met her were telling her what to do about her husband, her marriage and her future. “Getting all these opinions and judgments from the outside when no one really knows what’s going on,” she says. “Only the people that are in this know what it takes.” In November 2020, Hillsong founder Brian Houston told staff that Carl Lentz was out at the church’s Manhattan campus, citing breaches of trust. An extramarital affair had come to light. Laura, who had done nothing to land in that spotlight, found herself in it anyway. This month the two of them released a book, Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations To Help Heal the Hurt , and the couple sat down with us to talk about how they got from there to here. “I struggled with a lot of anxiety and just struggling with the opinions of others,” Laura says. “I had to really make sure that didn’t get in here and just remind myself that this is what matters and only we know what’s going on. Lots of therapy has been great. And Jesus, of course, helping through this.” The criticism hasn’t ended, but she says it has changed. “Now I find that’s really gotten quite silent. I think the fruit of our relationship and the fruit of our kids’ lives and where we are now and even writing the book, like you can’t not see God through our story. You can’t not see the miracle through our story.” She is clear about what the book is not. “We’re not out here promoting the book like we’re out to save marriages,” she says. “It’s about me healing, him healing and seeing where that takes us.” The Secrets That Started Small Asked what signs a young married couple should watch for, both of them go to the same place: secrets. “It’s not just big secrets, it’s like the little things,” Laura says. “If you can’t be honest or you’re hiding things from your spouse, those are dangerous and they just compound.” She remembers praying in the weeks before everything surfaced. “I don’t know what it is, but God, you’ve got to get this, just get it out.” Carl says the distance did not begin with the affair. “You don’t start keeping secrets about cheating. You start keeping secrets about fear.” He describes deciding what his wife could handle and keeping the pressure to himself. “It’s when I made the decisions for her on what she was capable of holding,” he says. “Then you stack them and you stack them. By the time you get to the horrific stuff, you’ve already got a pattern of hiding stuff.” What he tells young men now is blunt: get used to being vulnerable with your wife. “It turns out it’s very attractive.” He also rejects the idea that pastors have nobody to tell. “If anybody ever says ‘I didn’t have anybody to be open with,’ I lovingly say I don’t believe you. You chose to not tell anybody.” He says that if he had called Houston on a bad day, he would have been flown out to help. “I did not call. I was not honest. That’s on me.” What Staying Actually Looked Like People tell the spouse who stays that she is brave. Laura is not sure that’s the right word. “It’s so hard to stay, it’s so hard to go,” she says. “Yes, I was brave, I guess, but I was also taking a risk.” She says she would never tell someone to stay in an adulterous relationship, and that she herself saw evidence of change before she did. “There’s gotta be evidence of things that are changing for you to stay and he’s gotta be doing his work.” She describes the early days in small units of time. “We literally went one day at a time. I would wake up and go, okay, I can do today. And that was it.” Carl, a basketball fan, says she has learned the language for it. “Every day, I’m on a one-day contract. That’s an upgrade from a two-hour contract that I was on for quite a long time.” The marriage that came out of that, Laura says, is not the one they had before. “Marriage 2.0 is like so much deeper. Our marriage was fine, but it wasn’t like it is now.” Carl is careful to say it isn’t easy. Some da

articles.title: Meet Elle Limebear, the British Artist Who Turned a School-Assembly Hymn Into a UK No. 1
articles.summary: The daughter of Delirious? frontman Martin Smith rebuilt “Oil in My Lamp” for a new generation, and “Give Me Joy” has spent nine weeks atop the UK Christian chart.
articles.summary_zh: Delirious主唱马丁·史密斯（ Martin Smith ）的女儿为新一代重建了“Oil in My Lamp” ， “Give Me Joy”在英国基督教排行榜上排名第九。
articles.title_zh: 认识英国艺术家Elle Limebear ，他将学校集会赞美诗变成了英国第一
articles.content: Elle Limebear used to have a hard time describing her dad’s job. When classmates asked what he did, she’d say he was in a band, then that it was Christian music, then that it was sort of rocky, and then she’d watch the conversation go nowhere. Some days she wished he were “just a plumber dad.” Her father is Martin Smith, the frontman of Delirious?, the British band behind “History Maker” and “Did You Feel the Mountains Tremble?” and one of the defining worship bands of the late ‘90s and 2000s. She remembers touring the US as a kid, on big tour buses, with people lining up for photos with him. Back home in their English village, “no one really cared.” Limebear now lives in Brighton with her husband, Tom, and their three young children, and the song she’s best known for is one almost every British adult has sung. “Give Me Joy,” released in July, reworks the hymn “Oil in My Lamp.” It debuted at No. 1 on the Official UK Christian & Gospel Singles Chart and has held the top spot for nine weeks since. Decca Records, which announced her signing the same month, calls her its first contemporary Christian artist. The hymn was a fixture of British school assemblies, whether or not the school was religious. “If you sing ‘Oil in My Lamp,’ probably everyone will know it,” Limebear told RELEVANT. “It’s in our childhood. It’s in our bones almost.” She started slipping it into her live sets a few years ago. The reaction surprised her. “There was this eruption of, I know this. I remember being a kid singing this,” she said. “People just belted it, absolutely belted it.” Her husband suggested she rewrite it for people who never grew up singing it. Her first reaction was that the song was already a banner. “What a challenge.” She wrote new verses and melodies and kept the heart of it. When her new label asked whether she had anything to lead with, she figured the answer was no. “It’s a British kind of hymn-like thing,” she said. “Not super cool.” Then she played it for the team, a room of people who, in her words, don’t know Jesus. “They absolutely loved it and it brought them alive. They’re like, I remember singing this song.” The song was only a chorus and a verse at that point, and the response is what pushed her to finish it. Limebear never planned to be a songwriter. At 20 she was set on photography, which felt safe. “I could contain it, control it,” she said. Then she felt God tell her, clearly, to do music. “It didn’t feel like my thought.” She says fear kept her from believing she had anything to bring, and she didn’t know how to write songs. “Back then I was definitely hesitantly walking through these doors full of fear. Now I feel like I’m skipping through them.” The version of England she’s skipping through is a different one from the England she grew up in. She was the only Christian in her whole school, she said, and her youth group “saved my life.” Lately she hears from friends and church leaders across the country about people walking into church out of plain curiosity about Jesus. “There’s this thing called the quiet revival that they say is going on,” she said, “where people are just finding him in all sorts of places.” She remembers being the weirdest person in the room for it. Now, she says, people are discovering that “actually, being a Christian isn’t that weird.” Her takeaway for believers is the same one. “I think we should all be more curious, even as Christians,” she said. “Get more curious. Ask more questions.” Asked what’s behind it, she didn’t pretend to know. “I don’t know is the answer.” She pointed to decades of quiet prayer, from older women in church prayer meetings to families praying at home for relatives to come to faith, and added: “God hears every prayer, doesn’t he?” and “nothing’s wasted.” She also described the last few years in the Church as “good, sad, confusing,” with “lots of walls” coming down, and says she senses something being built back up that looks different from before. articles.title_zh: 你能在积累财富的同时仍然跟随耶稣吗？是的，但首先定义“足够”。
articles.content: The first decent paycheck can come with an unexpected side of guilt. Maybe your salary no longer starts with a 4, or your savings finally hit a number that once sounded rich. The relief is real. So is the question: Am I allowed to want more? For Christians raised to view wealth with suspicion, professional success can feel surprisingly complicated. The paychecks get bigger, but the question of what faithful ambition looks like often goes unanswered. Paige Whitaker thinks the question is worth asking, and that the guilt is pointed at the wrong thing. “I don’t believe wealth and purpose are competing pursuits,” says Whitaker, brand growth and partnerships manager at 316 Financial, a faith-forward bank. “Throughout Scripture, we see faithful people who were blessed with significant resources. The real question is whether we own our money or our money owns us.” Abraham was rich. So were Job, Lydia and Joseph of Arimathea. Scripture doesn’t treat having money and worshiping it as the same thing. Jesus put it plainly: you just can’t serve two. “Wealth becomes dangerous when it becomes our identity, our measure of success, or the thing we rely on most,” Whitaker says. Define “enough” before you get there One practical move: Define enough before your income makes it easy to keep moving the goalposts. “Purpose acts as a guardrail,” Whitaker says. “It helps us define ‘enough’ and reminds us why we’re pursuing financial success in the first place. Without purpose, it’s easy to spend a lifetime chasing bigger numbers while missing what truly matters.” Write it down. A number for the emergency fund. A lifestyle line you won’t cross even when you could. A giving percentage that goes up with your income instead of down. The point is to make the decision once, on purpose, so you’re not renegotiating it with yourself every time a bonus hits. Ask a different set of questions Building wealth with purpose, Whitaker says, starts by changing the questions. Instead of “how do I get more,” ask what the money is for. She points to serving others, providing for family, supporting churches and investing in communities and causes that matter. Run your own money through it. What does your current budget say you care about? If the honest answer is DoorDash and a car payment, that’s data, and now you know what to change. When the increase comes Markeia Johnson leads the Financial Stewardship Committee at 316 Financial, and she gets specific about what to do when the raise actually lands. “When financial increase comes, our response should be guided by prayer and purpose rather than increased spending,” she says. “Additional resources can be used to reduce debt, build savings, invest for the future, support ministry and help those in need.” Notice what’s missing: “upgrade everything.” Lifestyle creep is the quiet way money takes over. Every raise gets absorbed, enough keeps moving, and ten years in you make three times what you did and feel exactly as stretched. “Having the means to make a purchase does not always make it the right decision,” Johnson says. Money as a tool Both return to Matthew 6:33, where Jesus tells His followers to seek God’s kingdom first. “When we seek God’s Kingdom first, money becomes a tool for stewardship rather than a source of security or identity,” Johnson says. “True prosperity is measured not by how much we possess, but by how faithfully we use what God has entrusted to us.” “Money is a tool, not a destination,” Whitaker says. “Wealth is valuable because of what it enables us to do, not because of what it says about us.” Build wealth. Negotiate the raise. Learn how a Roth IRA works. But decide what the money is for before it starts making those decisions for you. “Wealth is a wonderful servant but a terrible master,” Whitaker says. “The goal isn’t simply to build more wealth. The goal is to use what God has entrusted to us to make a meaningful impact.” This article is presented in partnership with 316 Financial, a faith-forward

articles.content: In the NBA, the postgame TV interview moves fast. The horn sounds, the star of the night gets steered toward the sideline and a reporter is waiting with a microphone before he’s caught his breath. After the Toronto Raptors beat the Washington Wizards 112-102 on Friday, Oct. 23, the microphone was ready. But Scottie Barnes was walking across midcourt with a Gatorade towel over his head, headed for the Wizards’ postgame prayer circle. A player in the Washington group waved him over. Barnes stepped in among forward Anthony Gill and a handful of Wizards players, and the circle closed around him. Barnes, Toronto’s 25-year-old forward and a former NBA Rookie of the Year, had just finished with 28 points, 14 rebounds and five assists. Toronto’s TV broadcast, meanwhile, was holding for him. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bleacher Report (@bleacherreport) “He just took off,” one of the Raptors’ broadcasters said as Barnes joined the huddle. “So we’ll wait a minute for him to return.” A few seconds later, the call caught up to the picture: Barnes was “in the huddle there with the Wizards players, sharing a prayer as the Toronto Raptors come away with this victory.” When the circle broke, there were hugs all around, and Barnes started back across the floor with the towel around his neck. “Here comes Scottie,” the broadcast said, sending it down to the sideline. The microphone was still waiting. Gill, in his seventh season with Washington, was one of five finalists for the J. Walter Kennedy Citizenship Award in 2024, which NBA writers give for community service. He has talked publicly about his faith, too. Sharing the stage with Orlando Magic forward Jonathan Isaac at Liberty University’s convocation in 2024 , he told students that people assume an NBA player has “it all figured out.” “They assume that just because you’ve been blessed with a lot of money, life should be easy,” he said. He also said, “I tell myself I need to be more like Jesus. And what was Jesus? The ultimate servant. So, I serve the people around me.”

articles.content: Forrest Frank has released the first trailer for The Jesus Generation , a documentary about his record-setting Jesus Generation Tour. Lionsgate will distribute the film, which includes appearances by Rick Rubin, Philip Anthony Mitchell and Sadie Robertson, among others. Forrest posted the teaser to YouTube and Instagram, with a sign-up page for updates at forrestfrank.com . A director and release date haven’t been announced yet. The Jesus Generation Tour ran 29 cities from June 1 at the BOK Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to a sold-out finale at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, where more than 35,000 people came. More than 519,000 people attended in two months, which makes it the biggest Christian music tour in history. It also registered outside Christian music. One count named it the biggest arena tour overall. Pollstar ranked the tour No. 5 on its LIVE75 chart in late June, behind Bad Bunny, BTS, Luke Combs and Iron Maiden, who were all playing stadiums. Pollstar said it was the highest chart position of any artist booked primarily in arenas. Early reported shows averaged about 18,000 tickets a night. Hersheypark Stadium in Pennsylvania drew 27,365 people on June 15, and GEODIS Park in Nashville drew 23,667 four days later. Tori Kelly, Cory Asbury and The Figs supported the tour. Demand was there before the first show. Pollstar reported in December that the tour had already passed 470,000 tickets sold. The growth is steep. His first headline run, the 2024 Child of God Tour, drew 48,246 people over 17 shows. The following year, the Child of God Tour Part 2 drew 214,626 fans to 26 shows. This year’s tour more than doubled that attendance. The music behind it has been on a similar run. Child of God II debuted at No. 12 on the Billboard 200 and logged the most weeks at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Christian Albums chart. “Your Way’s Better” was the No. 1 Hot Christian Song of 2025 and broke into the Hot 100. Forrest has also placed 70 songs on the Hot Christian Songs chart, the most of any artist. Here is the teaser:

articles.title_zh: 购买10种主食需要美国人平均花费一小时的工作时间。在某些国家/地区，这需要超过19天
articles.content:
Ten basic foods now cost more than a week of work in 11 of the 56 countries surveyed in a new
Price Shocks report
from World Vision, and nine of those 11 are in Sub-Saharan Africa. In Sudan, buying them takes 19.3 eight-hour workdays. In Myanmar, 10.1, and in Haiti, 9.5. In the Central African Republic, buying them takes 30.1 days. In the U.S., it takes an hour.
Between November 2025 and May 2026, researchers priced the same ten foods at local markets, shops and supermarkets: a kilogram each of bananas, rice, wheat flour, sugar, maize and tomatoes, a dozen eggs, a liter of cooking oil, a liter of milk and one raw chicken. They then compared the cost of those ten foods with each country’s average income per person, adjusted for purchasing power, to work out how many hours of work it takes to afford them. That is a national average, not a minimum wage, so a lower-paid worker would need even longer.
Average income can hide inequality and may overstate what the poorest families can buy. Four countries with active conflict or collapsed institutions, South Sudan, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela, were left out of the hours analysis because there was no income data to compare, so the survey found bad situations but misses the worst ones.
Sudan shows how hard a conflict zone is to measure. The survey recorded the Sudanese price of the ten foods getting 36 percent cheaper than in 2024, yet the report says famine was present in parts of the country in 2025 and 2026, and Sudan is still one of the least affordable places in the study.
The report also profiles families living with the numbers.
Khin, 45, earns money ironing and washing clothes in Myanmar’s Yangon Region. Her husband can’t work because of poor health, and they have eight children. “There are days when my children eat rice with only oil and salt,” she is quoted as saying. “This is no longer occasional; it has become a daily reality.”
She says her twins are becoming malnourished and having digestive issues. Her 12-year-old daughter, Chit, told the report’s authors that fish and chicken have given way to spinach, tea leaf salad and fermented fish sauce.
In Hinche, Haiti, Cherlande runs a market stall that pays for her children’s school, their clothes and the family’s food, and she says she has no other income. A cup of rice that cost 20 or 25 gourdes now costs 50, she says, and a small packet of spaghetti has gone from 50 gourdes to 100. “You can’t afford to eat meat every day,” she said.
In 2025, an estimated 35.5 million children were acutely malnourished worldwide, nearly 10 million of them severely, according to the Global Report on Food Crises figures the report cites. Malnutrition can damage a child’s physical and cognitive development and weaken immunity, and the effects can last into adulthood.
The report asks governments, donors and businesses to protect children’s access to food during crises, expand school meals and social protection, and invest in local food systems.
Compassion International
works on the same problem from another angle, and says it provides children living in poverty with care that includes meals, tutoring and medical care.
TAKE ACTION
Read the
full report
, pass it to someone who has never thought about groceries in terms of days of work, and pray for the families behind the numbers.

articles.content: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include books about the Old Testament, Proverbs, faithful presence, the life and influence of Tim Keller, and a whole lot more. Westminster Books is continuing their Reformation sale by offering discounts on ESV Bibles as well as the tremendous new 500th anniversary edition of Tyndale’s New Testament. Recommended Reading How the Mainstream Recruits for the Manosphere. Aaron Renn explains how “asymmetric blame, hectoring lectures, and selectively revived norms are driving young men to the influencers the mainstream condemns.” How Mental Illness Became an Identity. Myles Werntz has an interesting review of a new book by Fredrik deBoer that explains how mental illness became an identity. “Mental illness in the 21st century is an expanding category—and one increasingly dominated by its most functional and therefore visible members. That displacement—in our collective imagination and public discourse—of the profoundly mentally ill by my college students didn’t happen all at once. And how did it happen? Was it because of the closure of traditional mental hospitals, like those of One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest ? Was it because of the internet-driven phenomenon of self-diagnosis by very functional influencers? The marginalization of psychiatry as a profession? Or denial, romanticization, and politics?” It Can Happen Here, Too. “As numerous countries in Europe experience riots, many in America are asking, ‘What on earth is happening on the continent that was, in many ways, the cradle of Western civilization?’ As historic buildings, places of worship, and commercial properties combust before our eyes on the nightly news, how are we to make sense of this?” Carl Trueman warns that what’s happening in Europe could also happen in the United States. 8 Ways to Help Your Kids Love the Church. Shiphrah Lakka offers a series of ways to help your kids learn to love the church. “While discipleship at home is extremely important and something every Christian parent should pursue, it can never replace the church. Reading Scripture together, praying as a family, and teaching our children about God within our homes are vital practices. Yet God’s design for believers extends beyond the walls of our homes. He calls us to belong to a community of believers who worship, serve, and do life together.” I Hate Your Halloween Decorations. Marc Sims writes about the reality of Halloween today. “The next time I am out, we will really slow down to take in the diorama you set up of black hooded figures encircling a pentagram-alter with a fake infant set in the middle of it, that way he can become familiar with Satanic rituals and child sacrifice. I mean, where else is he going to get this important cultural experience? Apparently, you are under the impression that becoming desensitized to violence and death is an important step for our whole neighborhood to take in—to celebrate, even. Here, frumpy old Marc ( boooo! ) was worried about why our culture seems ever more eager to relish death and the demonic—but you have shown me that this is really just fun! Save a fake a corpse for me!” Why Paper Books Endure. Daniel Darling explains his ongoing love for paper books (even while he’s not entirely opposed to electronic ones). “When I began my writing career in the early 2,000s, every single writing conference I attended featured speakers who issued grave warnings. E-books would eventually take over. Paper books would be a thing of the past. Libraries are nice relics of another era. articles.title_zh: 使用人工智能色情片是罪过吗？
articles.content: Over the past two decades, I have written a great deal about pornography . At many different times and in many different forms, I have urged people to consider a long list of arguments against it. I’m thankful to have interacted with many people who have come to see pornography as evil and who have committed themselves to sexual purity. Some of the strongest and most effective arguments against using pornography are based upon the humanity of the people who are involved in it. So, for example, in “ 7 Good Reasons To Stop Looking at Porn Right Now ,” I wrote that we need to consider the cost to those who make it. “Pornography exacts a high cost of those who create it—the cost to their bodies, to their souls, to their mental well-being, to their dignity, to their future. A vast amount of the pornography you enjoy is created by people against their wills. The simple fact is, by watching porn, you are watching rape and deriving pleasure from it. You become a willing participant in sexual violence and you allow that actor on the screen to suffer for your pleasure.” Even if some pornography is consensual, a great deal of pornography is not, and the viewer cannot know which is which. Similarly, in “ 8 Sins You Commit Whenever You Look at Porn ,” I said that those who watch it are guilty of sexual assault. “A person who drives a getaway car for a band of bank robbers will rightly be charged with murder for anyone who is killed in committing that crime. The person who voluntarily watches sexual assault for purposes of titillation is rightly guilty of that sexual assault. And a nauseating quantity of pornography is violent in nature, displaying men taking advantage of women. Sometimes these women have volunteered for such degradation and sometimes they are forced or raped into it. To watch such horrifying smut is to be a participant in it and to bear the moral blemish of it.” While these are far from the only arguments against pornography, I believe they are especially effective ones. But what happens when the characters involved in pornography are no longer people? What happens when they no longer exist at all, but are merely generated by AI? Could AI allow us to create “ethical pornography” that solves one of the foremost concerns that come with “real” pornography? In other words, is it a sin to look at AI-generated porn ? (For our purposes, we will assume that we are already rejecting deepfake porn—using the likeness of an existing person—as morally repugnant and both immoral and illegal. Instead, we are considering images of people who are generated entirely by AI.) The simple answer is yes: it is as sinful to look at AI-generated porn as it is to look at human-created porn. While some of the arguments may not be as relevant, the majority are unchanged. Before I explain how and why, I want you to listen to a warning: we are all experts at circumventing the spirit of the law by abiding within the strict letter of the law. There is something deep within us that wants to defy the rules that are given to us, and we become skilled at justifying the ways we do this. Often this involves reducing morality to a strict binary, then convincing ourselves that because we have not blatantly broken the law, we have abided by it. This was exactly the sin of the Pharisees of Jesus’s day who would strictly tithe the spices they grew in their gardens, yet fail to live according to the higher principles of justice, mercy, and faithfulness. There is something of the Pharisee in each one of us. With that in mind, here are reasons why it is a sin to use pornography that has been generated by AI. You are still lusting , even if you are lusting after a person who exists only on a screen. To lust is to long for an illicit sexual pleasure, and to long for an illicit sexual pleasure is to find satisfaction in what God has forbidden. articles.content: Good morning. May the Lord be with you and bless you today, my friends. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include lots of good books from New Growth Press and other publishers. Among them you’ll find several good options from Jared Wilson. Recommended Reading Goodbye, ‘Sam’s Club’ Megachurch. Hello, Stained Glass. Christianity Today reports on what I consider a welcome trend: church buildings that look like churches instead of warehouses. It begins this way: “Trinity Presbyterian finally has a church building of its own. That building has arches. And carved hammerbeams that tell the story of the Bible.” 3 Reasons Why Christians Should Lay “R.I.P.” to Rest. Nick Batzig thinks it would be best for Christians to lay R.I.P. to rest. “I’ve noticed something of a concerning trend over the past several years. It is the way in which believers speak about culture-impacting individuals at their deaths. Instead of simply expressing appreciation for their life and achievements, it has become commonplace for Christians to use the shorthand ‘R.I.P.’ (rest in peace) on social media when speaking of individuals in whose lives there was no evidence of saving grace at their death. At the risk of sounding ill-tempered, I wish to set out several reasons why I am troubled by this occurrence.” Go Deeper with Ligonier’s Grow App. Looking to put down roots in God’s Word? The Grow app from Ligonier Ministries gives you clear Bible teaching and guides your daily study for a deeper walk with Christ. Ministry Partners can also access the verse-by-verse notes from the Reformation Study Bible directly in the app and get reliable answers to their theological questions with the Ask Ligonier intelligent assistant. Not a Ligonier Ministry Partner yet? Try these features for 30 days when you download Grow and sign in. (Sponsored) Beauty Demands to Be Noticed. Michael Jensen is right: beauty demands to be noticed. He tells about people who understand the connection between beauty and transcendence and says, “Clearly, the reductive and polemical explanation of the atheists isn’t proving to be compelling. People can’t square their deeply felt experience of the world with that. To the people I’ve been speaking with, at least, the world simply cannot be reduced to its material components, nor can its coherence be explained by resorting to chance.” Aslan Sane: The Bowiefication of Narnia. I’ve got a pair of articles to share that comment on the forthcoming Narnia movies, each taking a different perspective. In the first, the writer remembers the old Narnia series from her childhood and bridges from there to what we know of the new one. She’s not impressed with it. Aslan and the Christians Who Can’t Be Enchanted. In the second, the author rebukes people like me (and the previous author) who have expressed concerns. He reminds us that it’s a movie for kids and that we don’t really know much about it yet. (I’d say he writes with some degree of exaggeration when he accuses me of losing my mind, but I’m glad to consider what he says nonetheless.) The Day of Pioneer Missions Is Not Over. articles.content: Tuesday is the day most publishers release their new books, so each week I let you know what has just come our way from the publishers I follow most closely. This week brings a substantial new commentary on the Westminster Confession of Faith from a whole team of Reformed scholars, an updated edition of a well-known apologetics book, a couple of books for kids, and a new edition of the ESV. In each case, I’ve included the publisher’s description. (This is a new feature I trialed last week. The response was positive, so I’m going to keep it going. I have tried to improve the format and layout to make it easier to read.) Books for Everyone Crossway The Westminster Confession of Faith A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application Edited by J. V. Fesko, John R. Muether, and D. In 1646, a group of theologians composed what is arguably the most comprehensive statement of faith, the Westminster Confession. Their efforts to preserve Protestant theology against opposing beliefs endured. Today, amid growing interest in Reformed Christianity, the Westminster Confession remains an indispensable guide for living out doctrine, worship, and church governance sola Scriptura, “by Scripture alone.” This essential collection of essays presents an accessible guide to the Westminster Confession of Faith for 21st-century readers. Each chapter is devoted to a section of the historic document, carefully studying its context, its significance to the faith, and its application, as well as any controversies. Clear, thorough explanations of principles, including the Trinity, creation, providence, baptism, last judgment, and more, make this the definitive guide on Reformed Christian doctrine. The essays are written by faculty from Reformed Theological Seminary in their areas of expertise, ensuring a trustworthy and high-quality text for church leaders, teachers and students of theology, and laypeople. Geisler and Frank Turek Endorsed by: Gavin Ortlund, Sean McDowell, Gregory Koukl, Alisa Childers, and Josh Howerton Publisher’s description To some, the concept of having faith in a higher power or a set of religious beliefs is nonsensical. Indeed, many view religion in general, and Christianity in particular, as unfounded and unreasonable. Frank Turek and Norman Geisler argue, however, that Christianity is not only more reasonable than all other belief systems but is indeed more rational than unbelief itself. With conviction and clear thinking, Turek and Geisler guide readers through some of the traditional, tested arguments for the existence of a creator God. They move into an examination of the source of morality and the reliability of the New Testament accounts concerning Jesus. The final section of the book deals with a detailed investigation of the claims of Christ. This updated volume with fresh arguments will be an interesting read for those skeptical about Christianity, as well as a helpful resource for Christians seeking to articulate a more sophisticated defense of their faith. articles.content: Good morning from somewhere in rural Colorado. I’m here for the next few days for meetings and training, as well as a bit of hiking and photography and, best of all, some quiet times of writing. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include O. Palmer Robertson’s two-part Christ of the Consummation , which was commended by, among others, D.A. Carson, Sinclair Ferguson, and Joel Beeke. You’ll also find lots of great deals from Zondervan from books that are related to Protestant theology. Recommended Reading Can a Christian Be Demon-Possessed? I know there are many people who are concerned that, even though they are Christians, they may still be possessed by demons. Anthony Faggiano explains why that is not a legitimate fear. “Desire entices us; yielding gives birth to sin; sin grows toward death. Satan can tempt us, but we remain responsible for our desires and decisions. We cannot blame an indwelling demon for what Scripture traces to our sinful hearts. Yet God hasn’t left believers powerless. Through his Holy Spirit, we can begin to put sin to death and walk in obedience.” 7 Keys for Thriving in Lifelong Ministry. I enjoyed reading Joel Beeke’s keys for thriving in pastoral ministry. “Looking back over my ministry over the long term is much more encouraging than looking at it in the short term. A long-term perspective helps me see those who have been saved by the Spirit through my sermons, those marriages that have been strengthened, and even the fruitfulness of elders and deacons who were unsaved when I arrived at my church 40 years ago but have since come to know the Lord personally, vibrantly, and experientially.” Why Does Everyone Else’s Life Seem Better Than Mine? There are some good insights in Zachary Conover’s article on comparison and envy. “Comparison has a way of making us dissatisfied with things we once received with gratitude. We can be thankful for our homes, our families, our work, and the opportunities God has given us. But then we see someone else’s life. We scroll through reel after reel, and suddenly our own begins to feel inadequate. Their opportunities seem greater. Their accomplishments seem more significant. Their circumstances seem more desirable. Am I the only one who doesn’t have it all together? Why don’t I have what they have? And without realizing it, we begin to measure the goodness of God toward us against what He has given to someone else.” Put the Destination in the Frame. John Seel has a guest piece on Aaron Renn’s Substack that offers some helpful points on the way we talk about young men. “We are talking about men incorrectly. We frame discussions of men in terms of problems – the ‘crisis of boys and men’ or ‘failure to launch’ – rather than the destination we want men to arrive at. If we want a different outcome, we need to change the frame of our discussions about men to center on the new reality we want to create. We need a frame that naturally leads us to answer the key question: What kind of men do we want our boys to become?” Welcome to the Valley of Pain. This article from The Atlantic points out, correctly, that the “safe internet” is shrinking and that we need to be more vigilant than ever. “For the next year or two, if not longer, the internet is going to feel a bit touch and go, and more dangerous than we’ve come to expect. ‘It’s going to feel like the sky is falling’ for a while, Prince said. There’s a decades-long backlog of bugs in software written without much review or scrutiny—which was more or less fine so long as there was a very small number of skilled hackers. Over the past two decades, companies, governments, and individuals have been lulled into a false sense of security: Most people don’t think twice about punching credit-card numbers into the website of a local restaurant or gift shop, or forking over a home address and phone number in just about any customer survey. But the internet was always a dangerous place. We’re just waking up from a trance.” Adoption Is Not a T

articles.content: I recently spent a couple of weeks preparing a great deal of fresh material for a weekend-long marriage seminar. Along the way, I often found myself convicted by the content I was preparing. As I readied myself to teach others, I had to consider the ways in which I needed to be a student before I should be a teacher. One area this proved true was intimacy in marriage—but a kind of intimacy I think many of us seldom consider. There is no doubt that marriage is meant to involve a husband and wife baring their bodies before one another, so that marriage is the context in which a man and woman can experience what it is to be naked and unashamed—to be fully bared, yet fully accepted. And because marriage is meant to be the deepest kind of unity two human beings can experience, it makes sense that there is a physical component to it through which two bodies are literally joined together. This is usually what we mean when we discuss intimacy in marriage. It is my understanding that this kind of intimacy, while real, is also in a way representative or symbolic. It is a demonstration of a unity between two people that is not merely body-deep , but fully soul-deep. Physical intimacy is both significant and essential to marriage, but it is not meant to be the sum total of the intimacy shared between a husband and wife. Yet as Aileen and I have interacted with other couples, we have observed that many husbands and wives find it easier to bare their bodies than their souls. Even as they routinely give themselves to one another physically, they can withhold a great deal relationally and emotionally. Even as they give themselves in free and joyful lovemaking, they can stop short of a greater baring, which is the baring of their souls and the revealing of the deep recesses of their hearts. As Aileen and I discussed this together, we had to conclude that this is something we are prone to as well. It’s not that we hold back shocking secrets or scandalous sins that would cause the other to recoil in dismay or disgust. It’s that we are both reserved people who find it hard to let another person in. We are both wounded people who have been hurt by those who have misused information we have revealed to them. And then I suppose we are both prideful or distrustful people who hold back the pieces of ourselves that we think might cause the other person to lower their respect for us. But by holding back, we are failing to live with full transparency and, therefore, failing to live with full intimacy. The baring of our bodies exceeds the baring of our souls. There is an irony to this, because I am convinced there is a deep longing within each of us to be known. We want someone else to know us as we truly are and to still love us and give us their approval. But even while we want it on one level, we resist it on another, because we wonder what that other person will think of us if they know our deep thoughts, our secret longings, and our hidden fears. We wonder if they will still respect us if they know what causes us to feel shame or express remorse. Perhaps we doubt they’ll still love us if they know who we are far beneath the surface. Still, there is this longing to be known, to be as bare emotionally as we can be physically—and still to be loved and accepted. It is this longing that we never address when we hold back from revealing who and what we truly are, when we refuse to foster a deep soul intimacy—an intimacy that is then represented by, rather than superseded by, sexual intimacy. So how can we foster this kind of baring? By letting our spouse really know us, which may mean creating times and contexts for lengthy, deep, and uninterrupted conversation. This will involve asking good questions and then listening attentively so we can come to a correct rather than trite or hasty understanding of what is being communicated. To really know and be known is the work of a lifetime. It is work, but work worth committing to. By assuring one another that no

articles.content: In my weekly Works & Wonders column, I combine a brief devotional with other interesting and uplifting bits and pieces I gleaned throughout the week. I hope you enjoy this week’s collection! It includes: What a God We Serve! (A Devotional) Ambient Earth Wildlife Photographer of the Year What Animals Can You Outrun? Who Would Have Dreamed 🎵 Bird Radio Who Is Like the Lord? 🎵 1. What a God We Serve! God has wisdom to know what is best and wisdom to know how to accomplish it by the best possible means. He also has power to execute it all. But we may wonder, as it pertains to us, what is his will? What does his wisdom determine is best? What is he accomplishing through the execution of his power? The book of Romans contains words of tremendous comfort: “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). God’s will is our good, which means that God’s wisdom and power are directed at accomplishing what is ultimately for our good, and accomplishing it all in the best ways. All the things we experience, all the things we undergo, all the things we endure, all the things we celebrate and lament, the things that make us laugh and cry—all of them are born of God’s love, directed at our good, and executed in a way that is nothing short of perfect. What a God we serve! And what a God we worship today. 2. Ambient Earth Ambient Earth is a great project! A guy named Seán Doran took 49,000 of Butch Wilmore’s photos taken aboard the International Space Station, then repaired, remastered, and retimed them to create an incredible 7.5-hour, 4K journey around the earth. He also added Chris Hadfield’s recording of the sounds of the ISS, which honestly gets a bit annoying, so you may want to mute it and then put on some nice instrumental music in its place. This is a great video to just leave playing on a TV in a public place. (While we’re on the subject of Butch Wilmore, he’s a believer and recently wrote Stuck in Space , which you may enjoy.) 3. Wildlife Photographer of the Year I always enjoy a good photography contest and, for whatever reason, this is the time of the year when many of them announce their winners. That’s the case with the Wildlife Photographer of the Year contest, which had 65,000 entries from 121 countries and territories. That link leads to The Atlantic ‘s gallery of highlights, though if you prefer to see the official site, you can find it here . As you’d expect, many of the photos are nothing short of stunning. 4. What Animals Can You Outrun? I suppose we all wonder at one time or another whether we would be able to outrun certain animals. The BBC did some research to find out which animals we’d possibly be able to outrun and the ones we definitely wouldn’t. Overall, the news isn’t particularly good. It’s a good thing God made us smart, since he didn’t make us particularly fast. See: The animals you can’t outrun – and the ones you can . 5. Who Would Have Dreamed Over a decade ago, Sovereign Grace Music released a Christmas album titled Prepare Him Room . I guess they have dusted off that album and decided to give it new life by recording a live version of it. I’m glad they’ve done so, because it has some really good songs on it. My favorite, and one we sing seasonally at Grace Fellowship Church, is also the first track they’ve re-released: “ Who Would Have Dreamed .” 6. Bird Radio Bird Radio is a neat concept—you simply tune in to hear the calls of different birds from all around the world. God displays his creativity in many different ways and the sheer variety of bird calls is a pretty impressive one. (Also on the subject of birds, did you know the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service maintains a feather atlas so you can learn about the ones you happen to find?) 7. Bonus: Who Is Like the Lord? articles.content: Good morning. This Weekend edition of A La Carte has some long-form content, some think pieces, some lists of the most popular articles from the week gone by, and a whole collection of recommendations from readers like you. Enjoy! Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include books on sexuality, forgiveness, Habakkuk, Revelation, and more. Recommended Reading Not everyone is familiar with the term concupiscence , but most of us are familiar with some of the debates surrounding it. For example, are our unholy desires sinful, or is it only sinful to act out on those desires? This question often arises when we discuss same-sex attraction. Writing for Logos, Mark Jones explores the concept of concupiscence from a Reformed perspective. In brief, concupiscence (concupiscentia) originates from the Latin verb concupisco, which means ‘to ardently desire.’ There are proper, non-sinful forms of desire, which we would call ‘non-sinful concupiscence.’ For example, Jesus said to his disciples, ‘I have earnestly desired [ἐπεθύμησα] to eat this Passover with you before I suffer’ (Luke 22:15). But because we live in a fallen world, concupiscence typically has in view sinful desire, and usually in reference to sinful sexual desires. Because sin is the privation (lack) of righteousness and proneness to evil, concupiscence involves not just the acts but the desire of the person. Sinful concupiscence can be understood from God’s moral law: ‘You shall not covet’ (Exod 20:17). Concupiscence: Are Our Unholy Desires Sinful? The Guardian tells a strange and twisting tale of a death, a scandal, and a desire for revenge, which it summarizes like this: “After his mother died, Otto became convinced he’d been wronged by the forensic investigators – and that one of them was a fraud. The truth was even stranger.” Here’s how the article begins: On a balmy, quiet evening in June 2020, Otto’s elderly mother, Doria, was fading in her Munich apartment. As she lay with her eyes closed, her pale face, framed by her white hair, was calm. Otto, masked, gloved and draped in a sterile apron, dozed in a chair beside her. Otto, who sometimes goes by the name Rainer, and whose last name is only known as “Z” because of Germany’s strict privacy laws, was a doctor who had cared for his mother for years, ever since she had suffered a stroke and moved in with him. He described the course of that night to me. He woke to the sound of her short breath and tried to sit her upright. Her eyes were shut, and her lips pursed. She stopped breathing. Otto reached for his phone to call for help, but then Doria opened her eyes and stared into his. She smiled, drew one last deep breath, shut her eyes again, and lay still. A Death, a Plagiarism Scandal and a Quest for Revenge: The Bizarre Tale of Otto Z. Jonathon Van Maren sees Beatrix Potter as an example of true conservatism, and explains why that’s the case in a really interesting article about the life of someone whose work we are probably all familiar with. There is a type of academic who can only get noticed by attacking the legacies of greater men and women, and a prime example was cited by Matthew Dennison in The Spectator in his essay “Don’t Cancel Beatrix Potter.” The beloved children’s author has become the target of “specialist in postcolonial literature” Dr. Emily Zobel Marshall, who hilariously claims that Potter failed “to acknowledge her indebtedness to an oral storytelling tradition of enslaved Africans working on American plantations” and that this contributes to “a damaging and recurring appropriation of Black cultural forms that continues today.” This is frivolous stuff, and Marshall’s claims are a parasitic attempt to gain fifteen minutes of fame by slandering a woman who cannot defend herself. Dennison handily rebuts Marshall, and I’m glad he did—but I can’t help but think that fortunately, some writers are uncancellable. Potter’s books have sold 250 million copies. Sometimes one word is all that stands between the truth and a lie, between life and death. In the Reformation, that word was sola , “alone.” At a time when leaders in the church claimed to speak for God, the Protestant Reformers reminded God’s people that Scripture alone is our infallible authority. While many people sought to work their way to heaven, the Reformers boldly proclaimed the only true gospel: salvation is by God’s grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, to the glory of God alone. articles.content:
I can’t quite decide: Has AI already been around long enough that we can say we’re now living in an AI world? Or is AI so new that it has still only made the smallest impact compared to what will be the case five or ten years from now? Regardless, there’s no doubt that AI is here to stay and that we will all need to learn how to live with it. Even if we choose to avoid using it directly, it is going to be a constant presence in the background of our lives as it becomes a core product for businesses, governments, and every other institution we rely on or interact with. In that way, there is no avoiding it.
A Christian’s Guide to AI
Pete Killingley
Buy from Amazon
(Affiliate links)
I would like to think time will prove that Christians are already thinking about AI in
a distinctly Christian way
. Those who use AI widely and those who reject it entirely are both under obligation to think about it well. Thankfully, we are quickly being resourced with helpful books that can guide us. The latest of these is Pete Killingley’s
A Christian’s Guide to AI: 12 Biblical Answers to the Questions We’re All Asking
.
In his book, Killingley does exactly what the subtitle states: he asks a series of questions about AI and then answers them in a distinctly Christian way. His purpose is neither to endorse AI nor to disparage it, but to help readers understand it and, therefore, rightly evaluate it before they integrate it deeply into their lives. Here’s how he introduces this book:
A common view of the church is that we’re always a few years behind the world when it comes to any cultural or technological change. Whether that’s true or not, we should be asking where we want to be as churches: at the forefront of the change or picking up the pieces of the people AI leaves in its wake?
As Christians, we do need to start thinking about AI deliberately. The fact that you’ve picked up this book means you probably agree. It would be so easy for us to split into our camps of tech-lovers and technophobes … and then use or not use AI as we each see fit. Because the Bible doesn’t give us a handbook for how to relate to AI, we would each create our own guidelines, often without a huge amount of thought.
But as I’ve studied AI over the last few years and given seminars on the topic to churches and church leaders, I’ve been struck that although the Bible doesn’t explicitly mention AI, it does give us an abundance of theological themes that help us understand the AI revolution. Whether that be our theology of humanity, of technology, of creativity, of work, of friendship or of the future, the Bible is not silent.
Indeed, it is not.
The book’s first chapter begins with the most basic question of all: What is AI? His definition is simple, and borrowed from David Betts: “a human-made simulation of intelligence in a machine.” Because AI is a mere simulation of intelligence, he suggests we read the acronym as “apparent intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence”—a surprisingly helpful tweak to the term. He explains the different forms AI takes and singles out large language models as the kind we use most often.
The second question deals with our humanity and asks what makes us different from AI. This leads to a discussion of man being made in the image of God and the necessity of holding a high view of our humanity. The next chapter turns to the nature of truth and explains some of the ways AI can distort the truth: through factual inaccuracies, flattery, and bias.
Further chapters offer hope for those whose jobs may be imperiled by AI and explain whether it is right to use it to create art. It then moves to some of the questions that are probably top of mind for the average reader: Can I have an AI friend? Can I use AI to help me with my essay? Should I use AI to help me write my Bible talk? Should I use AI to make important decisions? Can AI help us share the gospel? These are exactly the questions so many of us are grappling with as we see the capabilities

Good morning, my friends. Thanks for reading today’s A La Carte. I’m so thankful for the privilege of putting it together day by day, and I’m glad you’re willing to read it. I trust you’ll find something that blesses and encourages you.
Sales & Deals
Today’s

,

Recommended Reading
We have 10,000 Digital Guides; We Need Spiritual Fathers.
Zach Hollifield draws a useful comparison between ancient Corinth and today. “You and I live in a digital Corinth, and we too certainly have ‘countless guides in Christ’. Podcasts, social media accounts, YouTube channels, book authors, Xers, Substackers, sermons from celebrity pastors we care for more than the ones coming from the pulpits at our own churches—we have countless guides in Christ. More countless than the Corinthians could have dreamed of.”
You’ll Never Regret That You Did the Right Thing.
I often say “you’ll never regret the sins you don’t commit.” A positive way to express that is what Jacob Crouch communicates here: you’ll never regret doing the right thing. “Let me be the voice in your ear for a minute: Do the right thing. You will never regret that you did.”

Grow

Reformation Study Bible
and the Ask Ligonier intelligent assistant tool to get reliable answers to pressing theological questions. Not a Ligonier Ministry Partner yet? Try these features for 30 days when you sign in to the app. (Sponsored)
Reformed Doesn’t Mean Robotic: a Case for Expressive Worship.
Thembelani Maqajana writes about coming to Reformed convictions in theology, and then evaluating Reformed worship. “For many Africans, music and movement are naturally connected. Clapping, swaying, raising hands or moving rhythmically communicate joy, thanksgiving, celebration, and participation. We shouldn’t label expressive worship as mere emotionalism. The important question to ask, then, isn’t: ‘are people moving?’; but ‘what is motivating their movement, and is it consistent with biblical worship?'”
The Solitary Grief of Miscarriage.
Luke Fong and his wife recently suffered a miscarriage. He writes about the solitary grief of it, but also encourages Christians to break the solitude by letting others into their sorrow. “Grief must be shared, regardless of whether one feels as though one is imposing on another by doing so. One thing my wife and I have learned, or are learning, through this experience, is that we have to trust that those who are our brothers and sisters in Christ do truly love us. We must trust that love can bear burdens, because love draws us out of our sorrow and into the truth that we are known and bound together in Christ.”
The True Voice of Aslan.
In the context of the forthcoming Narnia movies, Steven West goes to the source, which is to say, to the works of C.S. articles.title: A Broken System Protects Traffickers, Not Girls
articles.summary: I’m often asked about the night I spent in a Southeast Asian jail alongside three young girls who had been exploited by sex traffickers. But the primary question isn’t about why I was in jail. Rather, why were those three girls in jail to begin with? Why them, and not the traffickers who had taken…
articles.summary_zh: 我经常被问及与三名被性贩运者剥削的年轻女孩一起在东南亚监狱度过的夜晚。但主要的问题不是我为什么入狱。相反，为什么这三个女孩一开始就被关在监狱里？为什么是他们，而不是抓走……的人贩子……
articles.title_zh: 破碎的系统保护贩运者，而不是女孩
articles.content: I’m often asked about the night I spent in a Southeast Asian jail alongside three young girls who had been exploited by sex traffickers. But the primary question isn’t about why I was in jail. Rather, why were those three girls in jail to begin with? Why them, and not the traffickers who had taken them from their families and sold them repeatedly for sex, turning their lives into a brutal nightmare? Why not the woman who had put tape over the mouth of the young girl so that the man who was raping her would not be disturbed by her screams. The system failed them. The brothel keeper was tipped off about their rescue operation, allowed to hide her crime, and told to dump the girls at a nearby bus stop. The police who should have rescued them instead arrested them on immigration charges. The trafficker walked free, while the girls were treated as criminals. As I sat with them that night, I longed for those girls to have never been taken to jail, much less a brothel. I wanted them to have always been at home with their families, going to school, and playing with their friends. I wanted them to have never been harmed in the first place. But the reality is, like millions of women and girls in our world today, they suffered the consequences of a broken justice system. And so, the reason I stayed with the girls is simply that the alternative was just too horrible. I preferred to be arrested myself rather than leave them vulnerable to further assault. But there’s an important detail to clarify: in the end, I did not need to stay the full night. Once it was clear I was not going away, the jailer himself took on the responsibility of assuring their safety. In a broken system, when even just one agent uses their authority for good, the door to justice begins to open. Shifting Power The very next day, my colleagues at International Justice Mission (IJM) and I were able to bring the girls to safety and long-term holistic aftercare. I continued to visit the girls for years, witnessing their healing as they moved into new lives of freedom. But nearly 25 years after that night in jail, the fight remains the same; we must not leave until those with governing power wield their power to protect the most vulnerable. If we fail to intervene for the women and girls being brutalized by violent criminals, including intimate partners and family members, the alternative is unconscionable. But when we do show up, we get to be part of shifting the levers of power. Entire systems – even the most corrupt and unjust – begin to change for good. In the 21st century, we must reckon with the reality that millions of women and girls are still not any more safe from violence than they have been in any previous era. It is still true, as it has been for decades, that one in three women will experience physical or sexual violence in their lifetime. Today, and in fact, every day, 140 women will be killed by their partners or family members. But far too often, law enforcement and other government actors appear to be on the side of violent perpetrators and other abusers, rather than those who are suffering violence. Whether it’s taking bribes to protect traffickers, criminalizing women and children who are being exploited, or allowing them to be intimidated into not reporting the abuse, agents of the law bear tremendous responsibility and opportunity to change the systemic violence they have enabled to perpetuate. Violent crime thrives on opportunity, and the argument for countering this could not be more clear: strengthening justice systems deters violence. When laws are enforced and traffickers and other abusers are held accountable, other perpetrators of violence are discouraged from committing similar crimes. I think of this as flipping the fear equation. When violent abusers begin to fear the consequences of law, women and children begin to live free from fear. In my work with IJM, I’ve helped build a model that has proved this theory of change. We’ve meticulously m
