featured.content: https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/23102213/effective-evangelism.mp3 In the summer of 2021, pastor Luke Peterson moved to Columbus, Ohio, to look for lost people. To find them, he joined a gym. He started building friendships. And then he began asking those friends if they wanted to come over. “Word started getting around—‘You’re not going to believe this, but Luke’s a pastor,’” he said. ‘It created some intrigue, and people started coming. I used to have a note in my phone of how many people came to our church because I went to CrossFit Grandview. It was up to like 60 or 70 before I stopped counting because it was impossible.” Peterson’s good at evangelism, and his church is too—last year, they welcomed around 500 first-time visitors. When he preaches, he knows about half his audience is probably unchurched. Pastor Luke Peterson (right) chats with Capital Church attendees / Courtesy of Capital Church Facebook This is unusual in a country where 40 million adults have stopped attending church over the last 30 years, and where 76 percent of pastors said “fostering connections with unchurched people” is a need in their church. Much has changed since the Billy Graham rallies of the ’60s, the door-knocking of the ’80s, and seeker-sensitive church billboards of the ’90s. In the past, “you could randomly walk up to the person pumping gas next to you and say, ‘Do you know Jesus?’” said Perimeter Church pastor Jeff Norris. “Could that still work? Sure. But more and more, we tell people to invite neighbors into their home. The reality is that evangelism is much slower, and more relational, than it used to be.” Today, people aren’t as likely to read the Bible, think it’s the Word of God, or go to church . But they’re also less hostile to Christianity than they were five years ago. And while they read the Bible less—especially in Gen Z—the trajectory is moving up . “We’re not past ‘my truth, your truth,’” said Rob Warren, pastor of Doxa Church in Madison, Wisconsin. “But people aren’t as sure that their truth is actually true.” These days, evangelistically effective churches are keeping evangelism front of mind in the way they preach, train, and encourage their congregations. They’re celebrating small wins. And they’re leading with a high view of Scripture, prayer, and God’s sovereignty. “We’ve seen all of our ministries grow—from kids to youth to college ministry to Doxa Church as a whole,” Warren said. “It’s not just one demographic of people who are getting saved. God’s doing something.” Times Have Changed Thirty years ago, evangelical churches leaned on programs like Evangelism Explosion or Continuous Witness Training to deliver evangelistic focus and training, church leader Thom Rainer said . Those structured initiatives fit well in a culture that was more Christian and more institutionalized—it took an average of 20 church members to reach one person for Christ per year. Today, it takes 50, Rainer said . “Evangelism efficacy, evangelism effectiveness, has definitely diminished.” That trend is likely to continue. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. featured.title: We Need to Know Our Reformed Roots
featured.summary: This volume is an invitation to rediscover that heritage and to find fresh encouragement in the faithfulness of God, who has sustained his church through the centuries.
featured.summary_zh: 这本书邀请我们重新发现这一遗产，并在神的信实中找到新的鼓励，神几个世纪以来一直支持他的教会。
featured.title_zh: 我们需要了解我们的改革根源
featured.content: What does it mean to be Reformed? The label is used frequently but not always carefully. For some, it simply refers to a particular view of salvation. For others, it evokes a tradition, a culture, or even an aesthetic. Yet historically, to be Reformed has meant something much richer. While no single sentence can capture the fullness of the Reformed tradition, at minimum it means three things: to be biblical, to be covenantal, and to be confessional. The authority of Scripture governs our theology, covenant theology provides Scripture’s redemptive framework, and the historic confessions summarize and safeguard the church’s doctrinal convictions. Remove any one of those pillars, and something essential to the Reformed tradition is lost. With “Reformed” in its name, it’s hardly surprising that Reformed Theological Seminary has long sought to equip pastors and church members in all three areas. In recent years, members of its faculty have produced substantial volumes on the Old and New Testaments and on covenant theology. Now, with The Westminster Confession of Faith: A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application , they turn their attention to the confessional foundation of the Reformed tradition. The result is a volume that seeks not only to explain what the confession teaches but also to demonstrate why confessional theology remains vital for the church today. What Is the Westminster Confession of Faith? The Westminster Confession of Faith takes its name from the Westminster Assembly, a gathering of more than 100 ministers and theologians convened by the English Parliament in 1643 at a time of profound political and ecclesiastical upheaval. The assembly was tasked with recommending reforms to the doctrine, worship, government, and discipline of the Church of England. After more than five years of careful biblical study and theological deliberation, the assembly produced the Westminster Confession of Faith along with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Together, these documents have served as the doctrinal foundation of Presbyterian churches throughout the world for nearly four centuries. The assembly’s influence, however, extends far beyond Presbyterianism. The confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. As a result, its theological influence shaped generations of Congregationalists, Baptists, and other evangelical Christians. The editors of this volume rightly observe, The confession is also ecumenical because it found wide acceptance among Congregationalists and Particular Baptists in the seventeenth century, as two different groups of theologians adapted the confession according to their theological convictions, producing the Savoy Declaration (1658) and the Second London Confession (1689). Thus the Westminster Confession is relevant to Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and Baptists. (xx) Why Another Commentary? The Westminster Confession has never lacked commentators. From the 17th century onward, pastors and theologians have written to explain its theology. Quality works by A. A. Hodge , G. I. Williamson, R. C. Sproul, and more recently Chad Van Dixhoorn have each served the church well in different ways. So why do we need another commentary on the confession, and what makes this one useful? The Westminster Confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. First, this isn’t the work of a single author but a collaborative effort by scholars whose expertise spans several areas of theology. That breadth allows the volume to approach the confession from different perspectives while maintaining a clear unity of purpose. Each contributor brings particular expertise to the section he addresses, but the volume as a whole is concerned with helping readers understand the confession and its significance for the church. Second, the commentary is consciously pastoral. Rath

featured.title: If the Church Did Its Job, Would the Parachurch Exist?
featured.summary: Do pregnancy centers, food pantries, or campus ministries exist because the church is failing to do her work?
featured.summary_zh: 是否存在怀孕中心、食品储藏室或校园事工，因为教会未能完成她的工作？
featured.title_zh: 如果教会做了它的工作，教堂会存在吗？
featured.content: I’ve heard it said more than once: “If the church did its job, the parachurch wouldn’t have to exist.” For instance, I was consulting with a local pastor who wanted to see the church serve people in poverty in his community. It was important to him that the church do it, not a nonprofit. Since he understood that God’s kingdom is bigger than his congregation, he wanted to engage multiple churches in the project. I suggested he consider forming a council of pastors and collectively hiring a staff member to manage the operations of the combined program. He thought that could work well for his context. I’m not sure he was aware of the irony. I certainly was: We’d just reinvented a variant of the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that he so keenly wanted to avoid in the first place. While the allergy to faith-based nonprofits was especially strong in his case, many people accept the premise at a basic level. In my experience, this sentiment is just as likely to come from someone who works in nonchurch ministry as from a pastor. If we understand the church is the core institution created by Christ to advance the kingdom of heaven, has it failed so badly that we need an army of auxiliaries to prop it up? Clarifying Terms and Roles I answer that the parachurch doesn’t exist because the church has failed. It exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. Proving that starts with clarifying terms. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. “Church” has more than one use in Scripture. In some contexts, it describes the people of God universally (Matt. 16:15–18; Eph. 1:22–23; Col. 1:18). In others, it’s a local congregational institution with the parameters God has placed around its operation (1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “Parachurch” typically refers to faith-based nonprofits who serve people in need or provide evangelistic and discipleship resources. Certainly, as part of the universal church, all God’s people hold equal status in advancing God’s mission, whether they labor as nurses, students, pastors, or tentmakers (see Acts 18:1–3). Just as surely, all God’s people shouldn’t merely attend but be accountable to a local congregation that enables their spiritual formation. When not assembled, God’s people are charged with many tasks—everything from stewarding creation to seeking justice for the oppressed. We can fulfill these tasks as individuals, but it often makes sense to create or join institutions dedicated to fulfilling them. Which brings us to a crucial point: God ordained some institutions specifically, and some emerged organically from God’s commands. Ordained or Emergent Institutions The family, the local church, and the government are ordained institutions. The Bible gives each ordained institution some guidance but also leaves a lot open to interpretation. While these ordained institutions are necessary for all people, they aren’t sufficient to fulfill God’s myriad commands to their fullest extent. Thus, some institutions emerge from the commands, rather than from a revealed institutional structure: The command to work led to the formation of businesses. The command to pass knowledge to subsequent generations led to the formation of schools. The command to care for the sick caused Christians to form the first hospitals. The command to care for the poor, widows, orphans, and strangers led to the formation of charities . The command to make disciples of all nations led to mission boards, publishing houses, and Bible-translation ministries. This ordained-emergent distinction parallels Abraham Kuyper’s “ sphere sovereignty ” in its recognition of institutions not explicitly outlined in Scripture. Many of these commands can be fulfilled to some lesser degree by the ordained institutions, but there are limitations. featured.summary_zh: 乔尔·比克（ Joel Beeke ）与马特·斯梅瑟斯特（ Matt Smethurst ）和利贡·邓肯（ Ligon Duncan ）一起探索清教徒可以教导今天的牧师关于祈祷、讲道、个人圣洁、牧养灵魂、处理批评和坚持传道。
featured.title_zh: 清教徒的教训（与Joel Beeke一起）

Drawing from decades of studying and teaching the Puritans, Beeke explains why they placed such a high priority on prayer, personal holiness, and applying Scripture to the hearts and lives of their congregations. featured.title: On My Shelf: Life and Books with L. Michael Morales
featured.summary: L. Michael Morales talks about what’s on his bedside table, favorite fiction, favorite rereads, and more.
featured.summary_zh: L. Michael Morales谈论他床头柜上的东西、最喜欢的小说、最喜欢的重读等等。
featured.title_zh: 在我的架子上： L. Michael Morales的生活和书籍
featured.content: On My Shelf helps you get to know various writers through a behind-the-scenes glimpse into their lives as readers. I asked L. Michael Morales—professor at Greenville Presbyterian Theological Seminary and author of Exodus Old and New: A Biblical Theology of Redemption —about what’s on his bedside table, his favorite fiction, the books he regularly revisits, and more. What’s on your nightstand right now? Malcolm Guite’s Galahad and the Grail . Myths of origin hold potential for shaping a society’s culture and character. I believe Guite, aside from writing good poetry and a national epic, is endeavoring to reawaken (or refound) England to her rich Christian heritage. This volume is the first of a projected four-volume work that may well represent the new definitive collection of Arthurian legends. Writings of the Ramban , translated and annotated by Charles B. Chavel. Nachmanides is my favorite medieval Jewish exegete and commentator, and these essays illumine his character and offer gleaming gems of insight. His essay on redemption, for example, gives a nuanced understanding of eschatology in the Hebrew Scriptures. He argues convincingly that the exile threatened in Leviticus relates to the Babylonian exile that occurred in Jeremiah’s day, whereas exile in Deuteronomy uses more eschatological language and seems to relate to the exile after the Second Temple’s destruction. Another essay records his Disputation in Barcelona, when Nachmanides was forced by the Spanish government to engage in debate with a Jewish Christian convert. The disputation eventually led to his exile from Spain since, as one of the intellectual giants of his era, he acquitted himself overly well. (Christian readers will, for the most part, be disappointed with the representation of our faith by his opponent, but the disputation is helpful in that it offers insights into the sort of questions about the Messiah we should think about more deeply.) What are your favorite fiction books? Aside from literary classics, I enjoy mystery books, especially medieval mysteries, although it’s hard to find good ones. Ellis Peters’s Brother Cadfael series is good, although aimed for a younger audience (and so a bit tame). She had a beautifully poetic sense of providence and justice, which makes for satisfying conclusions. I also appreciate the espionage genre, such as the early works of John le Carré, like The Spy Who Came in from the Cold , A Small Town in Germany , and Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy . Perhaps less thoughtful but often more fun, Alistair MacLean’s books never fail to offer a little escape into adventure. What biographies or autobiographies have most influenced you and why? Iain H. Murray’s two-volume biography of D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones had a profound impact on me as a young, inexperienced pastor—my copies are filled with underlining and scribbled notes. This account of the Doctor’s life and ministry not only led me onto the paths of the Reformed faith, but demonstrated God’s blessings on a faithful minister’s diligent commitment to the ordinary means of grace, to prayer and preaching. Many of the problems and challenges facing the wider evangelical church when I was pastoring had their roots in the era of Lloyd-Jones’s ministry, so reading his biography offered much-needed biblical wisdom and the discernment of hindsight. Augustine’s Confessions is also a treasured book—it’s so personal and honest, and displays the sure and gracious hand of God in one’s life. Confessions is also about Augustine’s mother, Monica, and how she persevered in prayer on his behalf; and about God’s faithfulness and goodness in answering her prayers so abundantly. Throughout the book, readers also get fascinating glimpses of life in the late fourth and early fifth centuries. What are some books you regularly reread and why? featured.title: How Can I Find the Motivation to Use My Time Better at Work?
featured.summary: Let’s start by counting the cost.
featured.summary_zh: 让我们从计算成本开始。
featured.title_zh: 如何找到更好地利用工作时间的动力？
featured.content: I work for a property management company that oversees retail space. I haven’t been doing this very long, but I’m finding that I’m not as productive as I’d like to be. Often, entertainment and fear of failure keep me from working. How can I get motivated to use my time better? Given that we’re to submit to our earthly masters with sincere hearts as unto Christ (Eph. 6:5), our productivity at work isn’t ultimately about our advancement or our employer’s success—it’s about our gospel witness. From before the fall, God ordained our work for keeping, cultivating, subduing, and exercising dominion over his creation. We’re still called to that today in any work to which we set our hand—including the property management of retail space. As believers, all work invites us to leverage our God-given talents and strength to bless and bring order to God’s creation in order to glorify him. When alluring distractions or a fear of failure hinder our labor, we can turn to him who calls us for the truth that will rightly spur us on. Distraction of Entertainment When entertainment distracts us from working, we should start by counting the cost. If we’re spending work hours on entertainment and then have to finish our tasks in what should be our free time, what else is this keeping us from stewarding well? It may be infringing on our time for relationships, spiritual disciplines, or true rest. On the other hand, if our working hours are fixed regardless of how on (or off) task we are, such as a job we clock in and out of with responsibilities only while we’re present, why are we willing to steal from our employer by accepting their payment without exchanging it for the labor we promised? Maybe we need to “cut off” what’s tempting us by blocking entertainment apps on our phone and computer during the workday (Matt. 5:30). If we’re spending work hours on entertainment, what else is this keeping us from stewarding well? Once we do, how might we instead faithfully devote that time to our employer’s good, even being willing to go a mile beyond what’s expected of us (v. 41)? Maybe we provide the talking points requested for a presentation—but also organize them into slides to save someone else from having to do so. Maybe we address the three issues our leader ask us to correct—but also address two more we discovered in the process. Perhaps if we worked with this level of diligence and care, like Joseph with Potiphar, we’d be given increased responsibility and influence that could be leveraged for the kingdom. Those who can be trusted with little can also be trusted with much (Gen. 39:1–6; Luke 16:10). Certainly, God would be glorified as we work with all our heart as to the Lord and not to man (Col. 3:23). Fear of Failure When a fear of failure keeps us from working altogether, we can start by digging out the root of that fear. Do you fear that your limitations and propensity to error will keep you from succeeding? Acknowledge that inaction guarantees you won’t succeed, but attempts to succeed in the work God has entrusted to you allow the opportunity for his power to be made perfect in your weakness (2 Cor. 12:9). When you feel discouraged by your insufficiencies, trust God to provide the wisdom and strength necessary for the work to which he’s called you—by prayer (James 1:5), the edification of his Word, and your humble pursuit of correction and growth through helpful resources and the example of others. Do you fear others’ judgment when you fail? Remember that your purpose is ultimately to please God, not man, and that there’s no condemnation for those in Christ (Rom. 8:1; Gal. 1:10). When you make a mistake or fall short of what’s expected of you, admit your error, seek understanding about what to do differently, and move forward with the humility and resolve that may make others respect you even more than they did before. featured.title: Simon Says: Inconspicuous Evidence of Eyewitnesses in Mark
featured.summary: Several features indicate that the eyewitness accounts of Simon stand behind Mark’s Gospel.
featured.summary_zh: 有几个特征表明，西门的目击者叙述支持马可福音。
featured.title_zh: 西蒙说：马可福音中不明显的目击者证据
featured.content: When I watch Jesus films, whether the current series The Chosen , The Passion of the Christ in the early 2000s , or even Godspell from the 1970s, I can’t help but ask, Where did they get those stories? Sometimes I can piece together bits from Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John. Occasionally I detect legendary material from church history or the apocryphal gospels. But at other times, my best guess is “They made it up,” and I ascribe the scene to creative liberty. When we turn to the Gospel of Mark, which most scholars see as the first extant telling of the story of Jesus, we might also wonder, Where did Mark get these stories? Around the 1920s to ’50s, the fashionable scholarly answer was found in a field of study known as form criticism . This enterprise tried to tie different sayings and stories of Jesus back to an occasion within the early church that would have prompted their creation. Though the heyday of form criticism has passed, the legacy of seeing the Gospels as a “mixtape” of various ad hoc literary traditions can still be seen today. In contrast to form criticism and the Jesus-film industry, the canonical Gospels are sourced in eye-witness testimony and were written within living memory of the events they describe. Perhaps no other scholar has written so persuasively on this subject as Richard Bauckham in his magisterial Jesus and the Eyewitnesses . Indications of eye-witness testimony are peppered throughout Mark’s gospel. Here we will consider just a few, each revolving around the name “Simon.” These are more obscure than what normally make their way into works on apologetics, but their subtlety is a strength since they are not the kind of details one fabricates. We will discover that inconspicuous indicators of eyewitnesses reveal what is happening behind the scenes more than front-and-center observations. Evidence of Simon Peter There are signs that Simon Peter has been a significant source for Mark’s Gospel, despite Mark not making a show of it. The church father Papias famously stated that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, who wrote down what he remembered from his preaching. Though many scholars doubt Papias here, Mark goes out of his way to emphasize Simon Peter. Several features indicate that Mark is particularly told from a Petrine perspective. For example, his prominence verges on redundancy when he is introduced in 1:16: “Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, [Jesus] saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.” This is part of what Bauckham calls a Peter inclusio, so that his testimony brackets the Gospel of Mark (see 16:7). Later in the narrative, those “sick or oppressed by demons” are brought to Jesus in Capernaum (1:32), the summary after the climactic exorcism at the synagogue (vv. 21–28). But sandwiched in the middle is the healing of Simon’s mother-in-law (vv. 29–31). Similarly, Mark writes of when the disciples look for Jesus, “Simon and those who were with him searched for him” (v. 36). Details like these betray a “Simon-centric” source. Bauckham argues that, with few exceptions, “Peter is actually present through a large proportion of the narrative from 1:16 to 14:72.” Several features indicate that Mark is particularly told from a Petrine perspective. An oddity in Mark’s grammatical style reinforces not just Simon Peter’s perspective but that of all the disciples: Mark uniquely favors using plural verbs to introduce singular ones. For example, Mark 11:12 reads, “On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he [Jesus] was hungry” (emphasis added). This provides the perspective of the group, as opposed to Matthew’s retelling: “In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry” (21:18). This literary device occurs 21 times in Mark’s narrative. Evidence of Many Simons The name “Simon” occurs 11 times in Mark. featured.title: Broken Bodies Make Beautiful Temples
featured.summary: We must view our foreign-feeling bodies as vessels through which God demonstrates his redeeming strength.
featured.summary_zh: 我们必须把外在的身体看作是神展示祂救赎力量的器皿。
featured.title_zh: 破碎的身体造就美丽的寺庙
featured.content: The Lord’s ways are not our ways (Isa. 55:8–9). Do we take this seriously, or do we revert to “our ways” in desperate seasons when we wander from God to seek meaning? I revisit this battle every time I look in the mirror at a quadriplegic body I desperately hope is not me. “Our ways” tell me that the body is incidental to identity. It’s an enticing lie that exploits disorienting bodily experiences such as disability , sickness, gender dysphoria, or other bodily insecurities hindering people from seeing meaning in bodies that feel foreign. I don’t see the nobility of God’s image or a temple worthy to house the divine when I’m being catheterized, bathed, or rolled in bed to prevent pressure sores. For others, disfiguration, tumors, or injury characterize bodies they can’t wait to “escape” at the second coming. For still others, their bodies contradict strong inward feelings telling them who they “really” are. Whatever the motivation, we tend to downplay bodily meaning when we feel it compromises our dignity. But this is autonomy’s way, not the Lord’s way. Scripture tells us there’s nothing undignified about weak, broken, dependent, or foreign-feeling bodies. The apostle Paul says our bodies (of all conditions) are temples of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 6:19). No higher calling exists for the physical than to serve as a temple to house its Creator. Paul’s claim is a hard truth for those with bodily insecurities, because it means we must trade the disdain we feel toward our bodies for contentment—a difficult but worthy exchange. ‘Glory of the Immortal God’ Paul is well acquainted with bodily fragility and limitations, yet he doesn’t hesitate to make the body central to the identity of people he calls “more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Rom. 8:37). For example, Paul observes in Romans 1:18–31 that the quintessential sin resulting from “exchang[ing] the truth about God for a lie” (v. 25) and “exchang[ing] the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man” (v. 23) is bodily sin that distorts God’s “very good” design for the body (Gen. 1:31). Thus, the “glory of the immortal God” of which Paul speaks is, at least in part, our bodies, which God created as his image (vv. 26–27). In Romans 6, Paul includes the body as part of the life Christ calls us to after “we have died with Christ” and subsequently “also live with him” (v. 8). He exhorts us to use our bodies “as instruments for righteousness” (vv. 12–13). Paul makes no exception for those with bodily insecurities. The body God gave you is an instrument for righteousness, no matter how broken or “inauthentic” it may feel. God’s Image, Not Ours Scripture teaches that my bodily self, no matter how foreign it feels, is me . And, like the rest of me, it doesn’t “belong” to me for two reasons. First, we’re not our own because the Lord makes his temples. Under the new covenant, “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands” (Acts 7:48), and the “Lord of heaven . . . does not live in temples made by man” (17:24). I did not make myself. The Lord “fearfully and wonderfully made” me; I am his “wonderful” work (Ps. 139:14) and “workmanship” (Eph. 2:10). He “formed my inward parts” and “knitted me together” (Ps. 139:13). Even brokenness, including disability, is the Lord’s wonderful work (Ex. 4:11; John 9:2–4). Second, we’re not our own because the Lord purchased us, body and all. Paul tells us bluntly, “You were bought with a price” (1 Cor. 6:20). A very high price: the death of his Son. My body is his, disability and all. Nothing about me is “mine” to do with as I please. My body is a temple for the Lord , not for me. He designed, constructed, and purposed it. “I” am no longer my own. Rather, my body is “meant . . . for the Lord, and the Lord for [my] body” (1 Cor. 6:13). My body is his, disability and all. Nothing about me is ‘mine’ to do with as I please. featured.title: What My Grandparents Taught Me About Pastoral Ministry
featured.summary: You’re being prepared for the work the Lord has for you in ways you may not understand until you’re standing in a hospice living room.
featured.summary_zh: 你正准备好接受主为你所做的工作，直到你站在临终关怀的客厅里，你才会明白。
featured.title_zh: 关于牧灵事工，我的祖父母教会了我什么
featured.content: When I was in high school, and early on during the summers in college, I spent my days working at a local pharmacy. I got a one-hour lunch break, and I ended up going almost every day to lunch at my favorite place: Granny and PawPaw’s house. I don’t remember how it started. One day, I drove over on my lunch break, and after that, it became my routine. They wanted to see me, and I wanted to see them. Sitting at their table instead of alone at a restaurant was comfortable and unhurried. At the time, I didn’t think much about it. I was just eating lunch with my grandparents. But looking back, I realize the Lord was doing more than I understood. Having now sat beside countless hospital beds and in living rooms with families walking through suffering, I can see how those lunches prepared me for ministry in ways I didn’t yet understand. My grandparents taught me how to slow down, listen, and simply be present with people. PawPaw When we ate, my grandfather talked mostly about his time serving in the Korean War, his years as an insurance agent for Liberty National, or fishing, which he loved almost as much as anything in the world. Courtesy Jared Cornutt Of the three topics, he talked about Korea the most. The war had ended decades earlier, but it hadn’t really ended for him. It shaped the rest of his life. PawPaw survived the war; he never escaped it. He talked around it in the way men of his generation often did when they carried wounds no one had given them language for. They wanted to see me, and I wanted to see them. At the time, I didn’t think much about it. I was just eating lunch with my grandparents. When I sat across from him at that table, I didn’t know what PTSD was. I just knew Korea was never far from his mind. Now I realize why. My PawPaw came home from the war during an era when PTSD wasn’t understood. Men like him were told to put the war behind them. They were expected to come home, go to work, raise a family, and move on. Many did. But many, like my grandfather, carried the war with them for the rest of their lives. As a boy, I didn’t understand that. I just knew him first as my grandfather, and I knew he loved me. I’m thankful that’s how I got to know him. Granny My grandmother had an tenth-grade education. She grew up on a farm in a poverty she also never fully escaped. She never had much of a formal education, but I can tell you this: She knew the Lord, and the Lord knew her. If you heard her whole story, you might call her life a tragedy. But due to her remarkable faith, she wouldn’t describe it that way. Courtesy Jared Cornutt I can still see her sitting in that rocking chair when I’d come over, reading glasses on and her Bible open in her lap. She was eager to tell me what she’d read that morning. She loved God’s Word because she needed it and depended on it. Every time I left her house, she’d tell me the same thing: “I’m praying for you.” That meant more to me than any gift she could’ve ever given, because I knew she wasn’t just saying it. She really was praying for me . I now know there was much about her life I didn’t understand. But what stayed with me was that my grandmother loved Jesus, loved his Word, and faithfully prayed for her grandson. The Lord didn’t answer every prayer she prayed the way she hoped. But I’ve often wondered how many of God’s kindnesses in my life came through Granny’s faithful prayers. Ministry Now I share all this because I recently sat in another living room. It was different, but it felt oddly familiar. As I left that room, it dawned on me almost immediately that I was equipped to minister there only because of those lunches years before. Every time I left her house, she’d tell me the same thing: ‘I’m praying for you.’ That meant more to me than any gift she could’ve ever given. featured.title: What You Should Know About the Hebrew Roots Movement
featured.summary: The Hebrew Roots Movement is a modern version of the New Testament Judaizers who were rebuked by Paul.
featured.summary_zh: 希伯来根源运动是新约犹太人被保罗斥责的现代版本。
featured.title_zh: 关于希伯来根源运动，你应该知道什么
featured.content: The hiss of the cappuccino machine filled the coffee shop, forcing him to lean in and raise his voice. “Show me,” he said, “where Jesus or the apostles ever told Christians they no longer had to keep the law of Moses.” I remember realizing that, if I were honest, I wasn’t entirely sure how to answer that challenge. I knew Christians weren’t under that law, but where in the Bible would I go to explain why? In the years since that initial encounter, I’ve had countless such conversations with Christians who have become involved in the growing restorationist movement most often known as Hebrew Roots. This movement teaches that Christians are obligated to keep the ceremonial law—especially the feast days, the dietary laws, and the seventh-day Sabbath. For most Christians, it appears out of nowhere. A church member begins lobbying for the Old Testament dietary laws. A spouse begins denouncing Easter, believing Christians are required to keep Passover instead. A small-group leader starts recommending YouTube channels that teach Christians are sinning if they don’t observe Shabbat . Before you know it, long-held historical Christian beliefs about the gospel, the church, and the new covenant are being openly challenged. These aren’t isolated stories. I regularly hear from pastors, leaders, and believers seeing Hebrew Roots theology sow confusion, strain relationships, and, in some cases, draw believers away from Christ’s sufficiency. They want to know what it actually teaches and why so many Christians are being drawn into it. And perhaps most importantly, how should pastors and church leaders respond? Hebrew Roots Defined To answer those questions, we must first understand what the Hebrew Roots Movement is—and what it isn’t. Over the past few decades, many Christians have grown disillusioned with shallow expressions of Christianity and begun looking for something deeper and more ancient. That desire has led some to seek out more liturgical and traditional Christian denominations. Others, however, are drawn to Torah-keeping communities, believing these groups more closely align with the beliefs and practices of the earliest Christians. But careful study of history shows that isn’t the case. Rather than uniting believers to ancient Christian practices, Hebrew Roots provides a highly diverse movement that emphasizes ongoing obedience to portions of the Old Testament . Before you know it, long-held historical Christian beliefs about the gospel, the church, and the new covenant are being openly challenged. The Hebrew Roots movement isn’t a monolithic organization. Most groups don’t even call themselves “Hebrew Roots,” preferring terms such as “Torah-observant,” “Torah-keepers,” or “Pronomian.” It’s a loose collection of teachers, ministries, and online communities that have emerged from mainstream Christianity and believe they’re recovering the “true faith” taught by Jesus and the apostles. The emphasis on recovering long-lost and hidden truths sometimes leads to highly individualistic interpretations among Hebrew Roots adherents. Despite their diversity, these groups share one central theological conviction: New-covenant Christians are required to keep the old-covenant law, and not doing so is sinful. This errant theology is commonly known as Torahism. Whereas the Torah (the first five books of the Old Testament) is a beautiful and fundamental part of the Christian faith, Torah ism is a dangerous misapplication of the old-covenant commands God gave to Israel. And if the theology sounds a little familiar, yes, this is a modern version of the beliefs taught by the New Testament Judaizers and rebuked by Paul in Galatians. It’s important to distinguish between Hebrew Roots and Messianic Judaism. The two movements are sometimes conflated because they look similar on the surface, but there’s an important difference: Hebrew Roots teaches Torahism ; Messianic Judaism doesn’t. featured.title: 7 Keys for Thriving in Lifelong Ministry
featured.summary: Learn long-term planning from Joseph, artful delegation from Jethro, lifelong consistency from Daniel, and aged wisdom from John.
featured.summary_zh: 从Joseph那里学习长期规划，从Jethro那里学习巧妙的代表团，从Daniel那里学习终身的一致性，从John那里学习年老的智慧。
featured.title_zh: 在终身事工中茁壮成长的7个关键
featured.content: At the starting line of an Olympic race, nothing looks particularly dramatic. The athletes stand still. The crowd waits. The runners’ muscles are motionless. The track lies open. Then the signal sounds, and in a matter of seconds the race is over. To the spectator, it may seem almost natural: a brief flash of speed followed by applause. But those few seconds are never merely a few seconds. They’re the visible tip of years hidden from public view. Behind that moment lie thousands of hours of training. Victory isn’t won merely by speed on race day; it’s won through long obedience before the race ever begins. If you’re a believer, you’re in a daunting spiritual race with eternal consequences. How much truer is this of the pastor, who also has the weighty task of shepherding other believers? If we want to avoid the all-too-common pitfalls of burnout, scandal, and disillusionment, we must follow seven keys to pastoral perseverance rooted in Scripture and biblical wisdom. Key #1: Radically Trust the Holy Spirit If we’re prone to neglect one person of the Trinity, it’s probably the Holy Spirit. This is a tragedy. If we can’t draw one breath of oxygen into our lungs without his aid (Ps. 104:29–30), how much less can we persevere in the ministry without his constant breathing of empowerment (John 20:22)? I wonder if one of the reasons for a high dropout rate among pastors is that we often try to do the Lord’s work without seeking his rejuvenating power. This divine power comes only through ardent faith and prayer. Oh, how we need conscious, wholehearted dependence on the Spirit! Those who sit under our ministry and preaching will be as dead as dry bones unless the sovereign Spirit breathes on them and transforms them into a mighty spiritual army (Ezek. 37:1–14; Eph. 2:1). Key #2: Pray Like Your Life Depends on It Prayer is the breath of the Christian and the heartbeat of persevering ministry. If you want to persevere, dear pastor, take every aspect of your ministry to the Lord in prayer—every sermon you preach, every class you teach, and every visit you make. Pray, pray, pray your way through the ministry! Oh, what sweetness you’ll find in sacred, childlike dependence on your heavenly Father. As John Calvin puts it , in prayer we climb into the lap of our heavenly Father and whisper our needs in his ear. Prayer is the breath of the Christian and the heartbeat of persevering ministry. As ministers, we must be much on our knees in prayer. Our method of study should be on our knees, then back to our books, then back to our knees again. We never do our theology alone; we do so in the presence of the triune God. Perhaps we don’t cry out to God more in secret—begging for his help in holy desperation and importunity—because we often don’t recognize how weak and needy we truly are. Key #3: Soak Up the Bible as Your Highest Calling As pastors, our power in public depends in large part on the quality and quantity of time we spend with God in secret (Matt. 6:6). We abide in Christ in proportion to the degree that his Word abides in us, and the Word abides in us in proportion to how much quality time we spend absorbing it—reading it, meditating on it, praying over it, memorizing it, internalizing it, preaching and teaching it, speaking it, trusting it, applying it, and fleshing it out through practical obedience. With the Spirit’s help, digest God’s Word with consistency, read it systematically, and absorb it experientially. Linger over every divine word. Bask every day in God’s presence. Cultivate holy familiarity with him. As you do so, your soul will be invigorated with life, strength, and vitality. featured.title_zh: 为什么转换原则对会员面试很重要
featured.content: Abstract: David Burnette explains why the doctrine of conversion is so crucial for pastors and churches as they carry out their responsibilities in affirming new members as believers. We must not only understand what conversion is but also be able to apply it to the lives of real people. After giving some basic reminders about membership interviews and identifying things that we are not looking for as evidence of conversion, Burnette provides four questions to help us evaluate whether a prospective member has been converted. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . “I wasn’t living right. I was getting drunk, partying, just doing whatever I wanted. And then it was like God just stopped me in my tracks. I knew something had to change. That’s when I started coming to church, and one Sunday, I felt like the preacher was talking directly to me. Right then I knew I needed to become a Christian, and I got baptized a few weeks later. That was about a year ago, and ever since then I’ve pretty much been coming to church and trying to do what’s right.” That’s how Ben responded when you asked him how he became a Christian. Ben recently moved to your city, and he just completed your church’s four-week New Members Class. Now, as the final step in the process—often called a “membership interview”—you as a pastor must decide whether you will recommend Ben for membership at the next members’ meeting. For the purposes of this article, I’m concerned primarily with the question of whether Ben is converted. I’m assuming he meets your church’s other membership requirements. No doubt you’ve heard similar testimonies, even if the details differ. There’s been some kind of change in the person’s life, and they seem sincere, but it’s not yet clear that this change was rooted in the gospel. So you’ll need to do some more probing. Putting Our Doctrine of Conversion to Work Testimonies like Ben’s remind us why having a biblical doctrine of conversion is so crucial when it comes to the church’s responsibility to affirm new members as believers. After all, it’s difficult to discern whether someone has been converted if you’re hazy on what conversion is . For an explanation of the doctrine of conversion, see Michael Lawrence, Conversion (Crossway, 2017); see also the article by Gregg Allison titled “You Can’t Make I t Happen: The Spirit and the Doctrine of Conversion” in this issue of Church Matters . Testimonies like Ben’s also remind us that we must be able to apply our doctrine of conversion to real-life people in real-life situations. Some prospective members will be new Christians, while others will be less mature in their faith; some will have been converted for years but still have significant blind spots; still others will think they’re Christians when they haven’t truly been converted. And those aren’t the only complicating factors. Some will have a hard time articulating the very truths they profess; others will fail to mention basic aspects of the gospel in their interview; more than a few will be unsure as to how and when they recognized their need for a Savior. All these factors (and more) mean that wisdom and discernment are needed when we are interviewing prospective members. Reminders for Our Approach Before thinking through some practical ways to probe further with testimonies like Ben’s, a few basic reminders may be helpful. featured.title: Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions
featured.summary: When we appeal to people’s carnal desires, we should not be surprised when our “converts” are more in love with the world than with our Savior.   The post  Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 不明确的传福音会导致不明确（和虚假）的皈依
featured.content: Abstract: John Lee explains how bad evangelistic methods and approaches can lead to false conversions. When we are unclear about the urgency of conversion, the cost of conversion, or the accountability that should accompany conversion, we risk leaving people deceived about their eternal state. Ultimately, our job is simply to proclaim the gospel clearly, trust God to open people’s hearts to the truth, and provide ongoing discipleship to those who respond in repentance and faith. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Maybe you’re like me and you grew up in a church that did altar calls. My church’s zeal for evangelism was real, and I can still tell you the names of individuals who came to know the Lord through those gospel presentations. But like me, you may also have walked down the aisle to accept Jesus as your Lord and Savior at least five times. The thing is, I believe I was sincere every time I walked the aisle. So why do it over and over again? There was clearly a misunderstanding, despite my church’s good intentions—and my own. The methodology of our ministry affects the fruit of our ministry. Or as Mark Dever has put it, “What you win them with is what you win them to .” Unclear invitations often lead to confused converts. Below I want to consider three different ways this lack of clarity in our evangelism manifests itself and how this can lead to conversions that, in time, prove themselves false. Unclear Urgency I was a disobedient kid. When my mother was particularly exasperated, she’d count down from ten. I had a choice: either obey or dig my heels in and rebel. But as I grew older, I became immune to her shot clock and more accustomed to her threats. My mom’s words fell on deaf ears. Bad evangelism capitalizes on this kind of “countdown” strategy. It puts eternity in the balance based on a singular moment and a one-time decision to follow God—or abandon him forever. And while unbelievers may initially respond positively, their “faith” often doesn’t last. As a result, they may become immune to the gospel because they assume they’ve already tried it. “But,” you might say, “isn’t conversion an urgent matter? Do we not care about people’s eternal destiny?” Absolutely! But we want to place appropriate pressure on their conscience, not just on their choice. Unbelievers need to make a thoughtful decision rather than simply meeting our demands in a singular moment in time. Panic urges them to turn off their critical thinking for the sake of survival. The focus is on an immediate decision rather than the weight of God’s eternal judgment. Unclear Cost At the same time, panicked evangelism is sometimes replaced with what we might call chill evangelism. Chill evangelism attempts to downplay urgency in order to make the decision to follow Jesus more palatable. To take one example, some recent invitations have defined following Jesus as “doing as he did.” The call is to adopt his behavior, particularly his compassion toward the brokenhearted. But following Jesus is about more than adopting a certain kind of spirituality and lifestyle; it’s also about salvation from the judgment of a holy God. Nor is it something you can dabble in; it requires real sacrifice. Jesus says in Matthew 10:38, “Whoever doesn’t take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” As Bonhoeffer famously said, “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship (Simon Schuster, 1959), 89. Conversion costs something. Saying yes to Jesus means saying no to sin, to our own passions, and to our former life. The question is: Does our evangelism draw attention to what people must give up? Conversion doesn’t propel us further toward our goals. Rather, it fundamentally reframes our goals in light of God’s kingdom. You feel sure that he is being genuine and so you pray with him and urge him to trust in Christ. Soon after, John tells you that he is now a Christian and so you put him in touch with a mature believer in the church to begin the discipleship process. As the weeks and months progress, you begin to observe a real spiritual hunger in John as he devours the Bible, attends a small group, and comes regularly to a class on Christian doctrine. John begins to pray earnestly in the public meetings, and he volunteers to serve the church body in a number of different ways. So far, so good. featured.summary: Rescue us from ourselves? No. Jesus died to rescue us from God’s wrath.    The post  The Reason for Church: A Review  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 建立教会的原因：回顾
featured.content: Abstract: Paul Alexander reviews Brad Edwards’s book The Reason for Church , highlighting strengths of the book’s cultural diagnosis while also identifying weaknesses in its prescription for how our current problems should be addressed by the church and the gospel. Edwards emphasizes how sin has affected the way we relate to one another, but he does not adequately address the way our sin affects our relationship with God. Readers will benefit from many of Edwards’s insights, but those who believe that the church’s primary mission is to make disciples through the proclamation of the gospel will find substantive areas of disagreement with his view of the church and its mission. Brad Edwards, The Reason for Church: Why the Body of Christ Still Matters in an Age of Anxiety, Division, and Radical Individualism . Zondervan, 2025. 240 pp. When many of us first read David Wells’s No Place for Truth back in the day, we felt like we did when we saw our first Trans Am. You know who you are—don’t deny it. I know, Christian cultural analysis is more than just “cool” or “awesome.” It’s public theology for evangelism. But shouldn’t it be at least a little thrilling to apply Christian logic to public trends? The world never tires of rephrasing the Serpent’s question, “Did God really say . . .?” Our age now rallies around a therapeutic spirituality, justified by victimhood as a new virtue, expressed through social media, aflame with anti-institutionalism. That leaves the local church looking so . . . 1900s, which implies we need not just a reason for God but a reason for church. The title of Brad Edwards’s book, The Reason for Church , tips us off that Edwards hews more to the apologetics of Tim Keller than to the systematics of David Wells. Edwards is an intellectually sophisticated critic of the meta-modern malaise. Thankfully, he loves Christ and the church more than anything in this world. He pastors The Table, a PCA congregation in Colorado that subscribes to the Westminster Confession of Faith. This book earned Christianity Today’s 2025 Book of the Year for its well-informed cultural analysis, penetrating insights, shrewd applications, and flecks of gospel gold. After reading it, I was not surprised to learn The Reason for Church also earned Edwards The Gospel Coalition First-Time Author Award. Edwards turns phrases like pancakes, but he’s not a show-off. He’s heartfelt, and he’s got personal stories from ministry in his own local church that verify and illustrate his analysis and applications. He writes like he’s done this before. Approach Edwards articulates his social critique of late modernity as Burkean conservatism, focused through the political lens of Yuval Levin and Jonah Goldberg, filtered through the sociological insight of Charles Murray, and lit by the psychological findings of Jonathan Haidt. The “little platoons” of local mediating institutions that put us shoulder to shoulder with people across the political aisle are disappearing (79, 93; think Putnam’s Bowling Alone ). We are fracturing the republic into politically homogeneous ghettos by ZIP code. With no buffer between the individual and the political, everything becomes political, impersonal, ultimate . . . and contentious. Diagnosis Today, individualism hijacks individuality such that self becomes sacrosanct. Boomers built churches on Peter Drucker’s pragmatism, which ended up offering Sunday consumers “a Coldplay concert with a TED talk” (14, 16). The church’s customer-is-king technique only manipulates our Main Character Syndrome, making church a provider of goods and services, and excusing us for treating each other as non-player participants in a reality where self is still the star of the show (47–48). Therapy teaches us to prize intuitional over institutional spiritualities (28–35, channeling Philip Rieff and Carl Trueman), so people retreat from churches that call them to repent, choosing instead safe spaces that affirm them in sin. featured.title: Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching
featured.summary: Worse than offending unbelievers is treating them like they are believers. Instead, we must aim to help sinners see their sin and confess their need for Christ. This spiritual clarity is not cruel, but kind.   The post  Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 在我们的讲道中瞄准皈依
featured.content: Abstract: Sam Romine argues that although the preaching that takes place in the weekly gathering should primarily be aimed at believers, pastors should also aim at the conversion of unbelievers in their preaching. He points as evidence to to the prophets of the Old Testament as well as the apostle Paul’s comments about the presence of unbelievers in the gathering in 1 Corinthians 14:23–25. Romine closes with three practical exhortations to help pastors put this into practice. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Some things are just meant to go together. A warm slice of apple pie with vanilla ice cream. Cozying up with a book on a rainy day. Watching fireworks light up the night sky with a grilled hot dog in hand. Preaching exegetically through a passage and calling for the conversion of sinners—well, that may be taking things a bit too far! As I’ve reflected on preaching with other pastors, it seems there’s a common temptation to underplay preaching for conversion while aiming to preach expositionally as though these two are incompatible or only awkwardly related. Why is this? Some are simply trying to guard against sloppy exposition that ignores the point of the text. Others have been scarred by past experiences of manipulative altar calls and forced invitations, so they seek to distance themselves from these methods. On the other hand, the failure to preach for conversion sometimes arises from biblical convictions. Since the church is for the gathering of believers, why should we take time away from them to tell unbelievers how to have their sins forgiven? Biblical Patterns and Grounds for Preaching for Conversion While I wholeheartedly agree that the Sunday sermon should primarily have God’s people in view, there is biblical precedent to aim for conversion in our preaching. Consider two examples: the Old Testament prophets and the apostle Paul. 1. An Observation from the Old Testament Prophets I love the prophets. They consistently leave me in awe of God’s majesty and glory, as God is shown to be holy and sovereign and, at the same time, kind and gracious. In this they provide a masterful example of how to weave in calls for sinners to repent while still speaking words of correction, comfort, and hope to believers. For instance, nearly all the prophets speak of impending judgment for Israel’s sin and promises of God’s future grace. Hosea pleads with Israel “to return to the LORD your God” (Hos. 14:1). In Joel, God urges the people to “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). Amos calls for the people to “seek the LORD and live,” (Amos 5:4) and Zechariah similarly adds, “Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3). Of course, Israel is not like the church in that God’s Old Covenant people comprised both believers and unbelievers. Yet we can learn from the way the prophets addressed not only the faithful among God’s people but also those with uncircumcised hearts. God’s concern for the salvation of sinners is demonstrated by repeated calls for repentance. 2. Paul’s Sunday Gathering Observation In 1 Corinthians, Paul addresses several topics pertaining to when believers “come together as a church” (1 Cor. 11:18). Here he makes an important yet often overlooked observation about these gatherings: we are to expect unbelievers to be present. Paul knows the church is made up of those who are “in Christ” (for example, see 1 Cor. 1:2, 4), yet he makes room for the attendance of non-Christians in the weekly gathering. We see this in at least two ways. First, he speaks of “outsiders or unbelievers” entering the gathering when the “whole church comes together” (1 Cor. 14:23). featured.title: Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship
featured.summary: Biblical friendship is not a luxury for pastors. It is one of God's ordinary means of sustaining us for long-term ministry.   The post  Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 田园友谊的八个敌人
featured.content: Abstract: Dave Kiehn argues for the importance of friendship for pastors while noting eight different “enemies” that can easily get in the way. These enemies, or obstacles, to pastoral friendships include things like pride, busyness, insecurity, and other issues related to the pastor’s heart and habits. Far from being luxuries, friendships are one of the means God uses to sustain pastors in their work. Pastoral ministry is often described as lonely, but, for most, it doesn’t need to be. From the opening pages of Scripture, God declares that it is not good for man to be alone. Throughout redemptive history, the Lord strengthened his servants through faithful companions. Moses had Joshua. David had Jonathan. Paul had Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Titus, Luke, and many other fellow laborers. Even our Lord surrounded himself with the Twelve and enjoyed a uniquely close friendship with Peter, James, and John. The church has long recognized the necessity of Christian friendship. Few, though, have captured the beauty of it better than J. C. Ryle: A friend is one of the greatest blessings on earth. Tell me not of money—affection is better than gold; sympathy is better than lands. He is the poor man who has no friends. This world is full of sorrow because it is full of sin. It is a dark place. It is a lonely place. It is a disappointing place. The brightest sunbeam in it is a friend. Friendship halves our troubles and doubles our joys. J. C. Ryle, Practical Religion: Being Plain Papers on the Daily Duties, Experience, Dangers, and Privileges of Professing Christians ( Baker Book House , n.d. ) , 336. Many others have echoed Ryle’s celebration of the blessing of friendship. C. S. Lewis famously observed, “Friendship is born at that moment when one person says to another, ‘What! You too? I thought I was the only one.’” C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves (Geoffrey Bles, 1960), 65. Charles Spurgeon added, “Friendship is one of the sweetest joys of life. Many might have failed beneath the bitterness of their trial had they not found a friend.” Charles H. Spurgeon, “ The Friend of God, ” in The Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit , vol. 33 (Passmore & Alabaster, 1887), sermon no. 1938. John Owen reminded us that Christ himself calls us his friends, John Owen, Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (1657). and Tim Keller observed that the entire history of redemption can be viewed as one great act of divine friendship. Timothy Keller, “Friendship” (sermon, Redeemer Presbyterian Church, May 29, 2005), Gospel in Life, https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/friendship-2/ . Yet if friendship is such a gift, why do so many pastors struggle to cultivate deep, lasting relationships? Sometimes it’s because of a lack of opportunity, though this seems rarer. More often, friendship is lost to enemies in our own hearts and habits. There are definitely more, but here are eight such enemies of friendship to be on the lookout for. 1. Pride: “I Don’t Need Anyone” One of the greatest threats to pastoral friendship, as with any kind of friendship, is pride. Pride whispers to us that mature pastors should be self-sufficient. It convinces us that asking for help is weakness and that admitting struggles will diminish our leadership. Scripture tells a different story. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Prov. 16:18). James reminds us that “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Peter illustrates this danger vividly. Jesus had told him and the other disciples that they would fall away, yet Peter confidently declared, “Even though they all fall away, I will not” (Mark 14:29). Within hours he denied Christ three times. Pride convinces us we are strong enough to stand alone. Humility invites other brothers to speak into our lives before we stumble and fall. featured.title: Youth Ministry Deconstructed
featured.summary: One way the church can minister to teenagers is by discipling their parents to be mature followers of Jesus.   The post  Youth Ministry Deconstructed  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 青年事工解构
featured.content: Abstract: Kyle Hoffsmith commends David Odom’s Youth Ministry Deconstructed , a book that helps churches evaluate and “deconstruct” their current youth ministry aims and practices in order to reconstruct their youth ministry in a way that is biblical, sustainable, and contextual. Hoffsmith highlights four main strengths of the book: it integrates youth ministry into the church as a whole; it encourages youth ministries to partner with parents; it encourages churches to evaluate their current practices; and it encourages churches to focus on spiritual growth rather than numbers. David Odom, Youth Ministry Deconstructed: Rethinking Your Ministry to Build Lasting Faith in Students . B&H Academic, 2026. 288 pages. There is much discussion today about what youth ministry should look like in the church. Some argue that teenagers should be fully integrated into the life of the church and treated as adults, which means that youth ministry (as it is typically understood) largely disappears as children get older. On the other hand, some churches believe that students should have their own age-segmented ministry throughout their high school years, where most of what is taught and planned is specifically for them. And there are plenty of positions in between. This isn’t merely a disagreement over church polity, as all churches must decide how best to minister to the teenagers among them. These young people need to be evangelized, taught, and shepherded in a way that helps them grow into mature followers of Christ “in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation” (Phil. 2:15). I would agree with professor, author, and youth ministry veteran David Odom that youth ministry needs a “deconstruction.” Odom uses this term as a play on words, as many today speak of “deconstructing” their faith. He uses it to exhort churches to tear down, or deconstruct, the structures and strategies they have used for decades to minister to teenagers. This deconstruction phase comprises the book’s first six chapters, as Odom offers metrics for evaluating your youth ministry in various areas, including spiritual growth, discipleship, and discipleship environments. Then chapters 7–10 focus on building back up, or reconstructing, your youth ministry in a way that is biblical, sustainable, and contextual. Church leaders will undoubtedly find places where they differ with Odom’s approach or his specific applications in certain areas, yet the issues and questions he raises are worthy of reflection. Rather than summarize each chapter, I want to commend Youth Ministry Deconstructed to church leaders by highlighting four main strengths of the book. 1. Youth Ministry Fits Within the Church as a Whole There has been concern for a while now about how youth ministry has created silos in the church. The most encouraging thing about this book is that Odom wants to integrate youth ministry within the church as a whole. So, for instance, when it comes to a question like, Should teenagers skip the corporate gathering to go to a youth worship service? Odom says, “Don’t allow a youth-only worship gathering to become a substitute for intergenerational corporate worship. Teenagers in the church benefit both young people and the congregation” (126). And when it comes to the question, Why does youth ministry exist? he points to an example of a student ministry that uses the following discipleship strategy: “The process for the student ministry is the same as the church as a whole” (112). This doesn’t mean that there can’t be spaces for students to learn in age-appropriate settings, but it does mean that churches should prioritize having youth in the main gathering. 2. Youth Ministries Should Partner with Parents This book emphasizes that youth ministries should partner with parents rather than simply connect with them. featured.title: Finish the Race: Final Steps in the Transition to a Plurality of Elders
featured.summary: It is easy to get lost in wanting to lead out in change just so we can say we did it, or out of concern to our reputation. But our motivation for change should be to bring greater glory to God and greater health to his church.   The post  Finish the Race: Final Steps in the Transition to a Plurality of Elders  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 完成竞赛：向多元长老过渡的最后步骤
featured.content: Abstract: Zach Kilpatrick encourages pastors who are transitioning to a plurality of elders to finish the process well by addressing some practical questions. Questions concerning how new elders will be identified, how they will be presented to the congregation, and what this will mean for the church’s existing constitution and bylaws—along with a multitude of other practical issues—may feel less important, but, as Kilpatrick reminds us in this third article of a three-part series, they are vital if the congregation is to have confidence in the men who are selected and in the process as a whole. Ultimately, this transition should be aimed at the glory of God and the building up of his people. You finally did it. You talked your wife into letting you turn the basement into a man cave! However, after receiving approval, you still have to do the work. What size TV will you buy? Where will it go? How much furniture will you have? Will you put anything on the wall? Many practical questions remain. Similarly, leading a change from a single-elder polity to a plurality of elders has final steps that are often overlooked. We know we need to educate the body on the biblical model and its practical benefits. We understand the need for discussions and an official vote. But even after all this, we aren’t done yet. Having discussed the evaluation and education phases of this process in previous articles, we will now look at the final step, which is also vital: execution. A Word of Warning: Remember Your First Love In his letter to the church in Ephesus (Rev. 2:1–7), Jesus commends them for their perseverance and discernment. Thomas R. Schreiner, Revelation , in ESV Expository Commentary , v ol. 12 , 570 – 571. They were known for their commitment to sound doctrine and righteous living. Yet they are rebuked because they had abandoned their first love. Schreiner argues that the Ephesians had stopped loving God and others. Sch r einer , Ibid. , 571. These Christians, who were so committed to doing the right thing, had forgotten why they were doing it in the first place. They had orthodoxy and orthopraxy, but they were missing love. Don’t let this be your story. It is easy to get lost in wanting to lead out in change just so we can say we did it, or out of concern to our reputation. But our motivation for change should be to bring greater glory to God and greater health to his church. So don’t lose focus after the vote is taken. See the process through to the end. Finishing Well Check Your Documents One of the first things to do after there is general agreement to move toward a plurality is to consult the church’s governing documents (bylaws, policies, and procedures). You need to determine how to officially adopt the change. Even if all the members are on board and ready, it still has to accord with your governing documents. If your documents do not allow for having a plurality of elders, then you will need to amend or rewrite them. The congregation will then need to vote to accept the amendments or new constitution. As part of this process, you might consider consulting a trusted attorney who has helped like-minded churches deal with these kinds of issues. They might have insights that help prevent you from making a costly mistake. Identify Elder Candidates Once your documents are in order, you will need to identify qualified elder candidates. How this process is handled will have a significant effect on the congregation’s confidence in the transition. One of the most important questions to answer is who will be responsible for nominating the first elders to serve alongside you. The constitution and bylaws of most elder-led congregational churches make the elders responsible for nominating new elders to the congregation. I think this is the best practice. featured.title: We Were Waiting to Die: Suffering as a Missionary for the Sake of the Name
featured.summary: I am here to testify that God is with his people in the midst of their suffering. Jesus promised to be with his people to the end of the age (Matt. 28:20), and he is faithful.    The post  We Were Waiting to Die: Suffering as a Missionary for the Sake of the Name  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 我们在等待死亡：作为传教士为名而受苦
featured.content: Abstract: Tyler Markson shares about his own experience of suffering as a missionary in Central Asia, including an occasion on which he and his teammates expected to die after a grenade exploded in their compound. Reflecting on his experience, Markson identifies four biblical realities of suffering to help missionaries and all Christians respond to suffering faithfully and with hope in God’s promises. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters , the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled “ The Pastor and Suffering .” “Death to Christians.” That’s the English translation of the phrase we found printed on a piece of paper and plastered to the large metal gate at the entrance to our Central Asian compound. My missionary teammates and I were returning from sharing a meal with friends down the street when we found this note around dusk. We snatched the paper off the gate and quickly made our way inside the seemingly secure walls of the compound. The death threat was not a total surprise. Over the last two years, I had grown accustomed to the uncertainty of living in an active war zone. Additionally, the preceding few weeks had been particularly volatile, as we had heard whispers from our local friends that we were no longer welcome in our city. We had gone up to the capital city for a week to let things cool down, and then four of us decided to take a two-day trip back to our home to test things out. It was on the second evening of this trip that we received the note on the gate. As we entered the gate and went through the courtyard, we immediately sat down in the living room to talk about next steps. Before we could begin talking, we heard shouting on the street. At the same time, we saw something thrown over the wall and land on the concrete porch mere feet from where the four of us sat, with only a glass window separating us. As soon as the object hit the concrete, I remember a deafening explosion and my entire field of vision was suddenly an orange-tinted color. I remember thinking, “A grenade just exploded. Did that really happen?” Waiting to Die It did happen. The glass shattered. We fell to the floor, crawled on our hands and knees to the bathroom, turned the light off, and sat in silence. We were stunned and unsure of what would happen next. But we all knew that in our country, attacks often started with a grenade and then people would rush in to finish what they started. We crouched defenseless in that bathroom in Central Asia. It’s the first time in my life I genuinely thought I was going to die. I remember many things going through my mind. I thought of my fiancée. I thought of my family back home in the U.S. I also distinctly remember thinking, “I never thought I would die crouched down in a bathroom.” But I also remember thinking, “If this is where the Lord has for me to die, then that’s okay. He’s worth it . ” For the next half hour, we quoted Scripture out loud, prayed, and waited for what we thought was imminent death. In God’s kindness, the attackers never entered our home. Four Biblical Realities of Suffering Well over a decade has passed since these events took place. By God’s grace, I write these words today from another Central Asian country, where I continue to live with my family and serve as a missionary. I have not experienced another incident of acute suffering like the one just described, but that doesn’t mean this last decade has been free from suffering. As I reflect on my own suffering as a missionary for the sake of the Name, I humbly offer four biblical realities of suffering that apply to all missionaries. 1. Suffering Is Normal Scripture is clear that suffering as a Christian is to be expected. “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you ” (1 Pet. 4:12). It’s easy enough to read these words, yet we often feel surprised when we encounter suffering. Missionaries enter cultures where Jesus

featured.title: Your People Need to Know the “Why” of Shifting to a Plurality of Elders
featured.summary: It seems the reason God gives pastors a job that is too big for one man is that he never intended for one man to do it alone!   The post  Your People Need to Know the “Why” of Shifting to a Plurality of Elders  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.title_zh: 你的人民需要知道转向多元长老的“原因”
featured.content: Abstract : Zach Kilpatrick encourages pastors to help their congregations see the need for a plurality of elders, first from Scripture and then from the various ways it can bless the church and its pastors. Many Christians aren’t aware of the Bible’s teaching about elders, nor do they recognize the strain that pastoral responsibilities can put on the pastor in a senior pastor model. In this second of three articles dealing with transitioning a church from a single-pastor model to a plurality of elders, Kilpatrick helps pastors think through educating their people on this important change. I never understood algebra until I took physics. Algebra was just abstract numbers until physics put those numbers to work. For instance, the quadratic formula helps determine how long a football can stay in the air and whether a receiver running at a certain speed could catch it. Now I’m interested. That’s what most people want—not just abstract theory but practical application. When leading a church through a major change, you should put both on offer. This article is the second in a three-part series on leading a church from a single-pastor polity to a plurality-of-elders model. As in the previous article, I’m using the terms “pastor” and “elder” interchangeably. In the first article , we saw the importance of evaluating your church’s history to help predict hazards you will likely encounter. In this article, we will see the importance of education in the transition process. Help Them See the Need from Scripture On the day of Pentecost, Peter told the gathered crowd to “Repent and be baptized . . .” (Acts 2:38). However, before he gave this command, he preached a sermon full of reasons why they should eagerly do so. In a similar way, we shouldn’t urge a change in polity until we’ve explained why that change needs to be made. Help your church see how a plurality of elders fits better with the teaching and example we find in the New Testament. Once they grasp the Bible’s model, adorn it with practical blessings that will come from adopting it—more on this in a minute. I’m convinced many Christians would be surprised to learn what Scripture actually says about polity. It’s simply too often assumed rather than understood. Therefore, we need to help our members locate the ecclesial prescriptions in their Bibles. Consider Paul’s example and instructions in Acts 20:17–35: elders should teach publicly and privately; teach believers and evangelize unbelievers; proclaim the “whole counsel of God”; know and care for all members of the flock; and protect the church against false teaching. According to Ephesians 4:11–12, elders are among those whom Christ has given to the church to “equip the saints for the work of ministry.” And when Paul tells Timothy the qualifications for being an elder, he says that elders should “manage [their] own household well,” “care for God’s church,” and be “above reproach” (1 Tim. 3:1–7). Given the breadth of these pastoral responsibilities, it’s not surprising that the New Testament repeatedly underlines there being multiple elders for each local church (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5; Jas. 5:14). Even on a practical level, a plurality of elders appears to be a more sustainable model for pastoral ministry. But if you don’t educate the congregation on these things, many will never see it. Help Them Feel the Need Once members understand the scope and difficulty of a pastor’s calling, they should begin to see that it is too big for one man, and I believe this is by design. It seems the reason God gives pastors a job that is too big for one man is that he never intended for one man to do it alone! Though we want to avoid coming across as complaining about our job, particularly given that many members also have difficult jobs, we can be honest with them about the strain of pastoring alone.
