featured.content: In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo Twenty minutes had passed already. The sun was going down, and they were looking everywhere, but they only saw men in the park. Sophia, an International Mission Board missionary, joined another IMB missionary and Maryam, a South Asian Christian. They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. Even if they went home without a single conversation, Sophia knew Maryam would want to try again. This woman who had grown up with a distrust of Muslims, now searched a park for a Muslim woman to tell about Jesus. When Sophia first invited her along, Maryam never imagined a Muslim could come to know Jesus. But the more they went out sharing the gospel together, the more God softened her heart. “One day, I found she was sharing in the park by herself, without me,” Sophia said with a laugh. These days, she shares regularly — with classmates, with rickshaw drivers, with women in the park, when she can find them. God transformed Maryam’s heart. He could transform this walk through the park, too. “So we stopped,” Sophia said, “and prayed, ‘God, give us just one woman to talk to.’” Then they spotted her — a girl sitting alone on a bench. Meeting the girl on the bench She looked like other conservative Muslim women in the area, covered in black except for her face. They approached casually, not wanting to frighten her. It was Eid al-Adha – “one of the biggest Muslim holidays here,” Sophia said. They greeted her and asked about her holiday plans. Her name was Tara, and she wasn’t intimidated at all. “You may think I’m a Muslim from the way I dress,” she said, “but actually in my heart, I have left Islam.” “I was a little shocked,” Sophia said, hearing such a bold statement from a stranger. Tara told them she was a university student at a conservative Islamic school, but she had grown disillusioned and discontent with the religion. “ I don’t believe in Islam anymore,” Tara said. Without knowledge of God, she had no one to pray to, and it left her lonely. She’d been searching — Buddhism and Hinduism from friends, even a meeting with atheists, who struck her as unhappy, following only themselves. “Do you know any Christians?” Sophia asked. “Would you like to hear what we believe?” “Sure, please share.” They read about Jesus’ birth, and Tara was hungry for more. When she asked about church, Sophia described their congregation of about 40 believers, many from a Muslim background. Though she wasn’t ready to visit the church, Tara continued her interest in learning. Sophia and Maryam met with her every week in coffee shops, tea shops, Sophia’s home, wherever they could talkthat wasn’t too loud or have “too many ears and eyes” observing them. Finding her closest friend They read through the Gospel of John. One November day in a coffee shop, they reached the passage on the Samaritan woman at the well, and Sophia noticed Tara was crying. “Tara, I see you have tears,” Sophia said. “Let’s stop. Let’s talk about it .” That day, Tara prayed to receive Christ. Soon after, she wanted to visit the church, though nervous how believers would receive her in a hijab. “They will love you,” Sophia told her. “Don’t worry.” Tara went and was welcomed. That Christmas, 80 people packed Sophia’s apartment, singing and dancing in circles. Across the room, Sophia saw Tara, wearing red Christmas garland like a scarf and a smile stretched across her face. “Tara grew up very conservative – music was not even allowed in her home. But now she’s dancing, worshiping the Lord with us with music and songs.” In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo That spring, Tara was baptized.

featured.content: The eastern face of St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City in Rome, Italy, is famous for its central balcony from which popes give their papal addresses. Most people in Rome have at least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” IMB Photo In the city where Jason and Lizzy Davis serve, some steps have a lot of meaning. And the meaning is different for them than it is for the thousands who travel there to visit that site. “If you come to Rome, you can come to a place called the Holy Steps,” Jason said. “People go there, and they’ll crawl up on their knees and pray the rosary all the way up.” From the top of the steps, a mural depicting Jesus on the Cross looks down on those making the pilgrimage. For Jason and Lizzy, it’s a spiritual experience, a picture of a religion that asks people to earn their way to Jesus. “That’s really the opposite of what the gospel is. The gospel is Jesus saying, ‘No, you can’t do it . . . no matter how good you think you are,’” they said. Most people in Rome have at the very least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism, as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” Jason explained, “It’s where the Pope lives in the Vatican. It’s very much part of the religion and culture. It’s all intertwined here.” An ‘unavoidable’ call Jason and Lizzy are investing their lives as International Mission Board missionaries in Rome, Italy, to share the truth of the gospel. The Davises partner with national believers through a new church plant, and they’re seeking to plant more churches within the city. Lizzy said for her, the call to missions was unavoidable. “I grew up as a third culture kid, or a missionary kid. My parents were on the mission field, as were my grandparents, all with the International Mission Board.” Then her family moved to Virginia for her dad to work for IMB’s home office staff. As a middle schooler and high schooler, every time Lizzy heard about the need for the gospel to go forth, she felt a burden, a “burning” in her heart. She didn’t know what God would do with that, but she had a feeling she would see one day. Now, years later, she and Jason spend their time trying to find as many opportunities as they can to invite people into their home so they can share the hope of Jesus with them. That can mean Bible study or simply sharing a meal. ‘Completely lost’ Jason has been surprised by just how often people are willing to talk about faith. “You can get into spiritual conversations very quickly with people, especially if you’re just open and honest with them.” Lizzy shared that one of the easiest ways to do this is to be willing to let your day be interrupted. “That’s something I’ve seen Jason do firsthand in our neighborhood. He walks down the street, and everybody knows him because he stops and takes the time to ask them questions about their families, gets to know people, gets to know the newspaper stand guy and the guy at the fruit stand and the grocery store ladies.” She emphasized that caring about people is “what Christ would do.” The Davises, whose previous mission service prevents their photos from being published, live in a neighborhood of about 130,000 people. Their church of 15 people is the only evangelical congregation there. Lizzy said the area is “truly a lost, completely lost, dark neighborhood” with people who have never heard the gospel. Thousands more come to their area on a religious quest. The Davis family’s neighborhood is home to the Basilica Papale di San Paolo (the Papal Basilica of Saint Paul), one of the city’s four major basilicas. “So we get a lot of people coming on spiritual journeys, visiting our neighborhood, seeking some sort of spiritual experience. And oftentimes it’s just trying to earn their salvation,” she added. featured.content: Rebeca Couto poses with her IMB teammates. Couto is a global missionary partner serving alongside IMB missionaries in Japan. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto poses with her violin. Couto is a professional violinist who is serving as a global missionary partner with the IMB in Japan. Doors have opened for her to use her skills with evangel ical Japanese musicians who perform. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. She is one of few, if any, believers in the Azores with such a long spiritual lineage. This rich legacy shaped her and prepared her for ministry. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ to be missionaries, wherever they are, whatever they’re doing, and whatever God has equipped them with,” Couto said. Couto’s great-grandfather became a Christian through the witness of missionaries from the United Kingdom. Later, missionaries from the Foreign Mission Board, now the International Mission Board, started the first Baptist work in the Azores by planting an English-speaking church near an American military base. A Baptist Brazilian couple planted a Portuguese-speaking church, which became the congregation where Couto grew up and was commissioned as a missionary. Ministry has been passed down through the generations of her family. Couto’s father has pastored for 20 years, and both of her parents have been involved in ministry for most of their lives. Couto now serves in Japan as a global missionary partner, a missionary who is financially supported by a sending church or organization in their home country and serves with IMB teams. Close to 400 GMPs currently serve on IMB teams around the world. Language learning Couto is immersed in language study in Yokohama, Japan. She had a head start before she even arrived. After graduating from high school, Couto moved from the Azores to Lisbon to pursue a degree in music. She spent hours on public transportation and wanted a challenge to pass the time. She decided to study Japanese because she thought it sounded beautiful. At the time, she had no intention of becoming a missionary in the traditional sense. However, the more she learned about the language and the culture, her burden for the lost grew. She began researching Christianity in Japan. “I understood how bleak the scenario was, and how much the country needed Jesus. I struggled with that calling because the doors were closed, and it didn’t seem possible to come to Japan for a myriad of reasons,” Couto said. After finishing master’s degrees in music and violin performance, along with a seminary degree, Couto was considering pursuing a Ph.D. or returning to seminary when her seminary professors, IMB missionaries Jonathan and Bethany Sharp, contacted her about serving as a missionary in Japan. They introduced her to the GMP program and invited her to attend a missions immersion school they piloted . Rebeca Couto (far right) poses with her IMB teammates. Couto is a global missionary partner serving alongside IMB missionaries in Japan. featured.content: Men and women gather to discuss spiritual topics with Caleb and Carina Beaty, International Mission Board missionaries who serve in Madrid. IMB Photo Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise when they arrive. Caleb said he always has a list of questions that begin broadly and funnel into questions such as, “If there were a God …” or “What do you think Christians believe about that?” or “Why do you think religions have such different perspectives?” The Beatys’ goal in these conversations is to work toward deeper worldview questions within 45 minutes to an hour. Most of the people who attend their Meetup group are from Madrid, but they also have conversations with people from other countries. During one Meetup, Caleb and Carina shared how creation was perfect, but sin led to a world separated from the Father. God offers salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus, they explained. “There are times we’re able to get to a clear gospel presentation with a group of people, and sometimes we’re doing pre-evangelism.” Caleb said. Some repeat attendees who have been attending for more than a year quickly jump to the heart of the discussion. “All right, Caleb, what’s the Bible say about suffering?” they’ll ask. Caleb and Carina then have the opportunity to share the Christian perspective. IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty and their children pose for a photo in a park in Madrid, Spain.  IMB Photo Spain has secularized rapidly since the 1990s, Caleb said. While many may think of it as a Catholic nation, many people do not know the basic tenets of Christianity. “We’ve got all the churches, we’ve got the cathedrals, and they do processions, but the average person on the street does not know anything about the gospel and does not know anything about Jesus,” Caleb said. Younger Spaniards are drawn to their group and are receptive to the gospel because they don’t have a spiritual foundation or know anyone who does. “There’s just this curiosity because, for a lot of them, they’ve never met someone who actually believes that God exists, and that changes your life,” Carina said. “I’ve had people completely shocked that we believe in God. ‘You really believe that God exists?’ They can’t wrap their mind around that.” During one Meetup, a man contrasted Protestant and Catholic beliefs by saying Protestants focus on Jesus’ suffering and Catholics on Mary’s grief. Caleb responded that evangelicals focus on the resurrection. When Caleb said Jesus rose from the dead, the man replied that he needed to look into that. Caleb said encounters like that reveal how little many Spaniards know about the gospel. Caleb noted the irony of the man’s sharing the Catholic perspective without truly understanding it. He is not the only person the Beatys have met who has missed the heart of the gospel. A friend of the Beatys told them she’d heard Jesus died, but she hadn’t heard he rose from the dead. A man reads a passage of Scripture during a Bible study hosted by IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty at their family’s apartment in Madrid, Spain. Five atheists began attending their Bible study after attending the couple’s Meetup group. IMB Photo The Beatys also host seasonal outreach events through the Meetup. Members from their church in Madrid have started attending the Meetup to learn how the Beatys lead discussions. Their group has become so popular, a waitlist has formed. Caleb and Carina host a small-group Bible study in their home. Five atheists who joined their Meetup now attend the Bible study.

featured.content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. To go along with the increased giving totals to the SBC’s missions offerings, Southern Baptists have also increased their local outreach efforts, indicating that the focus is not just on giving but on sending. Baptism totals have increased in each of the last five years, recovering from the pandemic-year low in 2020 to surpass the 2017 total. The five consecutive years of increase marked the first such streak in approximately 75 years. To Jordan Adams, unheard of things like 38 baptisms in one worship service have become “heard of” for his congregation. featured.content: Staff members at First Baptist Church in Wagoner, Oklahoma, evaluate their church’s involvement with missions and missionary support. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. For IMB missionaries Peter and Katie Weeks, that clarity is especially valuable. They participated in the lab alongside church leaders. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. featured.title_zh: 数字化之门为东南亚岛民打开福音之门
featured.content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. featured.content: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technology, K-cosmetics. Yes, good things… But many Korean people are struggling right now.” The Sols, who were featured in the 2025 Week of Prayer for International Missions , continue to rely on the prayers of faithful Southern Baptists. Prayers sustain them and help to push back the darkness they confront in their home culture. Hun often describes that hidden struggle with a Korean word: han. There is no simple English translation. It speaks to a deep sorrow shaped by generations of war, division, loss, and the quiet resolve to endure. Hun sees it in the young adults he meets every week—people navigating loneliness and relentless expectations, quietly asking what their lives are for beneath a veneer of success. Han is heavy. For many young adults, that weight can feel unbearable. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among teenagers and young adults in South Korean. Hun and Eunjoo see the effects of that reality every day, and it’s one reason they believe they have no time to waste. That understanding shaped the week of Serve Tour Seoul this summer. There were no construction sites, no paintbrushes, no tools or work gloves. Instead, the team stepped into ministries local churches had been faithfully building long before the volunteers arrived. In May, 27 volunteers from seven churches across the United States came alongside local churches already serving their communities in Seoul, Paju, and Gwangju. They taught English classes, ran children’s camps, walked neighborhoods in prayer, distributed food, and sat down with college students, one conversation at a time. For Nick Holst of Sandals Church in Riverside, California, the goal was simple enough to say in a sentence: “We came to meet people,” Holst said. “We want to hear their stories, and that leads to some very meaningful connections as you get past the surface into something deeper.” That’s where the week actually lived: past the surface and past the small talk, where the quiet weight of han is often carried without words. On college campuses, volunteers played games, asked questions and mostly just listened. Some conversations lasted a few minutes and ended there. Others kept going long past the point where either person expected them to. One morning, after asking his church back home to pray, Holst sat down with a university student named Intec. They talked about culture first, the way strangers do, and then the conversation turned somewhere neither of them planned. “I got to ask him, ‘What do Koreans believe?’” Holst recalled. Intec said he didn’t believe in God. Then he recited John 3:16 from memory, word for word, a verse he’d heard somewhere along the way and never forgotten. Before they parted, Holst asked if he could pray that God would keep drawing Intec toward Himself. “He said yes.” In a city where many conversations never move beyond the surface, the exchange was a reminder of why the team had come. Not to win an argument, but to listen, to ask questions, and to trust God with what happens next. The same pattern unfolded elsewhere, beginning in classrooms and ending on city streets. Jeremy Doyle, missions pastor at Valley Baptist Church in Bakersfield, California, watched an English conversation club grow from two students on its first night to eight by the second. Nobody advertised it as anything more than a place to practice English, but the room kept filling, and so did the conversations. The team’s work with students didn’t stop there. The award recognizes individuals who demonstrate exceptional leadership and creativity in advancing missions through innovation. Photo provided Don Barger, director of innovation and artificial intelligence for the International Mission Board, received the 2026 Excelerate Award from Missio Nexus during the Mission Leaders Conference, Sept. 24 in Orlando, Florida. According to Missio Nexus, a network of mission-focused organizations and churches, the Excelerate Award recognizes individuals who demonstrate exceptional leadership and creativity in advancing missions through innovation. Barger has earned a reputation for identifying emerging technologies and applying them to ministry challenges, helping pioneer the use of artificial intelligence in global missions while promoting a biblically grounded approach to innovation. Barger said receiving the award was both surprising and encouraging. “I realized it was an affirmation not only of my work, but of the work our entire team has been doing,” he said. “It’s encouraging to see the IMB recognized as an organization willing to invest in innovation, think creatively and explore new ways to reach the nations.” Barger has served with the IMB for 29 years in a variety of roles. He was involved in church planting and led indigenous work in Mexico and Central America. Most of his work as a missionary focused on oral learners and Bible storying. Long before artificial intelligence became mainstream, Barger and his team began examining its potential for missions. IMB team members developed a framework to guide appropriate and inappropriate uses of AI in ministry settings. One principle that continues to shape that framework is Barger’s conviction that “souls should care for souls.” “We do not use AI for counseling or to replace human spiritual care,” Barger said. “Instead, we use AI to handle tasks that free people to spend more time ministering directly to people.” While much of his work centers on technology, Barger emphasizes that innovation extends far beyond technical advances. He defines innovation as a willingness to ask new questions and explore new approaches while remaining faithful to biblical truth. “Too often the response is, ‘That’s not how we’ve always done it,'” Barger said. “Innovation that advances the Great Commission begins by asking new questions and exploring new possibilities.” Barger noted that Christians have a long history of embracing new tools to support gospel ministry, from the printing press to broadcasting and healthcare advances. As artificial intelligence continues to generate discussion among ministry leaders, Barger encourages both optimism and discernment. He points to AI’s potential to improve communication, accelerate training and remove barriers that can hinder ministry efforts. At the same time, he cautions leaders to recognize the limitations of AI and ensure people remain responsible for ministry decisions and engagement. “Every tool throughout history has been capable of both good and evil,” Barger said. “The opportunity is to use AI for redemptive purposes.” Barger’s work includes developing faithbot.tools , a collection of AI tools designed for evangelical Christians. Throughout his career, he has advocated using technology not as an end in itself, but as a means of strengthening ministry and supporting relationships. Looking ahead, Barger hopes his greatest contribution will be encouraging future mission leaders to think creatively while remaining committed to God’s mission. “I hope mission leaders develop a mindset of curiosity,” he said. “Instead of simply accepting, ‘This is how we’ve always done it,’ I want them to ask, ‘How might we do this better?'” For Barger, innovation is ultimately about stewarding available tools in ways that help advance the Great Commission. featured.content: Communication staff at 18 Bible translation organizations across Africa need professional training to tell God’s stories well. In November 2026, a one-week workshop in Ruiru, Kenya will teach practical skills like writing, photography, design and video. Then, six months of follow-up support will continue to strengthen networks and create a collaborative culture of sharing God’s stories widely and effectively. Project Name: Africa Area Communication Capacity Building Workshop Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance – Africa Area Contact: Phil Prior Director for Communication Wycliffe Global Alliance phil_prior@wycliffe.net Matthew Bore Project Funding Manager Wycliffe Global Alliance matthew_bore@wycliffe.net Start date: September 2026 End date: March 2027 Summary Across Africa, God is moving. Communities are receiving the Bible in their own language for the first time. Lives are being transformed. But too often, these stories never become known beyond the place where they happen. Why? Because not enough people are trained to recognise and report these stories to a wider audience. Among 18 Bible translation organisations across Africa, communication staff are doing their best—but without formal training in news writing, interviewing, photography, video and social media. Many also work in relative isolation without the chance to exchange ideas and collaborate on stories. The result: Amazing stories remain untold, and the people who could be praying, giving or getting involved never learn about the opportunities. This project changes that. For one week (2-6 November 2026) in Ruiru, Kenya, communication staff from those 18 Wycliffe Global Alliance organisations will come together — not just to sit in a classroom, but to actually create. Using smartphones and free tools, they will learn to capture the moments that matter: local communities and churches collaborating; a translation team’s challenges and creative solutions, groups engaging with Scripture, lives being transformed. Attendees also will build plans for how their organisations will keep telling these types of stories long after the workshop ends. Then, over the ensuing six months, this same group will keep coaching, encouraging, and learning from each other — turning 18 separate voices into one strong, unified story of what God is doing across Africa. featured.content: A three-year training program will prepare local translators across Southeast Asia to put the Bible into spoken forms—like storytelling and song—for communities that share knowledge by voice, not writing. Three workshops will build translators’ skills from basic to advanced to mentoring, so at least 20 participants gain local expertise. Project Name: Training Oral Translators Across Southeast Asia Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance Contact: Evelyn Gan Consultant for Oral Translation Programmes Wycliffe Global Alliance evelyn_gan@wycliffe.net Start date: FY 2026 End date: FY 2028 Summary Across Southeast Asia, many communities pass along their culture through spoken word—storytelling, song, and drama—rather than through reading and writing. For them, hearing the Bible in these natural forms often connects more deeply than a printed text. Oral Bible Translation is expanding rapidly in Southeast Asia, but the region lacks enough trained people to sustain it. Seminary graduates know the Bible but not oral translation. Practitioners already working need a path to advance their skills. And almost no one is ready to step into consultant roles. Without urgent, structured training, this shortage could stall Oral Bible Translation projects across the region. This three-year project will trains local translators and seminary students in oral Bible translation. Participants move through three stages: a foundation workshop, an advanced workshop and consultant-level training, with only those who show strong skills advancing to the next stage. Our goal is for at least 20 participants, with a smaller group becoming fully qualified to guide future translation projects. Half of the trainers will themselves be new, gaining experience so the program can continue and grow after this project ends. By working in collaboration with Wycliffe Thai Foundation, Wycliffe Malaysia, YWAM Chiang Mai, FCBH, Spoken Worldwide and CRU, the project is rooted in strong partnerships that will ensure sustainability and local ownership. featured.title: Bible translation’s future is diverse … and local
featured.summary: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding.
featured.title_zh: 圣经翻译的未来是多元化的……和本地
featured.content: Yaoundé, Cameroon — The landscape of global Bible translation is undergoing a paradigm shift, moving away from traditional, agency-led book printing and toward multimodal translations driven by local communities. At a June 2026 gathering in Yaoundé, translation partners and members of Wycliffe Global Alliance organisations spanning Africa, Europe and Latin America reflected on how Scripture is delivered in the 21st century. Their consensus: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding. Community-led translation Dr. Paul Kimbi, the Alliance’s Consultant for Bible Translation Programmes, said Bible translation’s future belongs to community dialogue rather than isolated translation agencies. This emerging approach, known as conversational translation, prioritises localised, grassroots work: listening intimately to communities, engaging them in active storytelling and using locally adapted communication channels. As multiple translation agencies increasingly operate within the same borders, global leaders are urging a shift toward radical collaboration. ‘The multiplicity of agencies is not a hindrance; however, harmony and unity are essential,’ Kimbi said. ‘Unity does not mean uniformity. Each agency, according to its unique strengths, approaches Bible translation as a collaborative piece of God’s global mission.’ Multimodal translations will better serve people from different contexts . Beyond the Book: Multimodal and AI Integration Because cultural contexts vary wildly across the globe, the Alliance’s Africa Area gathering highlighted the urgent need for ‘embodied and multimodal’ translations. This means managing multiple streams of communication simultaneously—integrating oral storytelling, vibrant illustrations, written text and digital media. ‘We do not communicate only with words; we communicate with colours, images, and multimedia,’ Kimbi said. ‘We can no longer consider translation strictly as a written book, but rather as a dynamic multimodal experience.’ This digital evolution naturally intersects with the rise of artificial intelligence. While delegates recognised AI’s immense potential to increase translation speed, optimise efficiency and lower operational costs for minority languages, attendees maintained a stance of strategic caution. ‘Technology accelerates the advancement of Bible translation and language development, but it also creates new strategic responsibilities for leaders and organisations,’ said Etienne Ondoa, a language technology consultant. Staff capacity building, therefore, remains the greatest investment, he said. As technology evolves, the skills required to support it in ministry also evolve. ‘Technological leadership should have a voice in strategic decision-making processes, Ondoa said. ‘Technological decisions increasingly influence ministry outcomes, sound financial resource management, cybersecurity, AI adoption and organisational resilience.’ Etienne Ondoa A Symphony for the Global Church Ultimately, leaders at the event reaffirmed that translation organisations do not operate in a vacuum. They exist to serve the church, which remains God’s primary vehicle for global mission. Kimbi likened the future of the movement to a grand, global arrangement. ‘The particularity of modern Bible translation is that it is a diverse ensemble—an orchestra of varied influences interpreting a magnificent symphony titled ‘Scriptures’ for every language community,’ he said. ‘And in this orchestra, we need everyone: local churches, oral communicators, media creators, literacy specialists and technology partners.’ Story: Lune Prudence Mvondo and Isaac Forchie Photos: Isaac Forchie
featured.author: Jim Killam

featured.title: God’s mission in Africa: ‘There is still much to do’
featured.summary: For both the African and global audiences at the Yaoundé gathering, panel members underscored a fundamental truth: Bible translation is not an isolated academic exercise.
featured.title_zh: 神在非洲的使命： “还有很多事情要做”
featured.content: YAOUNDÉ, CAMEROON — During the Wycliffe Global Alliance Africa Area Gathering, a question was put before delegates: Is the African Church awake? A three-person panel, moderated by Dr. Zac Manyim, Director of the Department of Church and Scripture Engagement at CABTAL (Cameroon Association for Bible Translation and Literacy), delved into the continent’s strategic mission challenges and local breakthroughs. A Call from the Pulpit to Action ‘Yes, the African Church is awake, but it is not active,’ said Rev. Abel Chebe Ngah of the Apostolic Church in Cameroon. He noted a disparity in how modern ministry resources are being spent. ‘Some churches are focused on building megachurches, while only a few are focused on spreading the Word of God. The African church should have been doing exploits, but it is not yet doing so. There are still many areas in Africa not reached by the gospel.’ For the landscape to shift, Ngah argued that mission cannot be treated lightly; the local church must intentionally send missionaries. Demonstrating local ownership, his own denomination dedicates a specific Sunday every year entirely to Bible translation, using it to mobilise believers and raise financial support for CABTAL’s fieldwork. Though some local churches might lack the required financial resources, they offer abundant human and material resources needed in Bible translation. The Lifelong Impact of Mother-Tongue Literacy Pastor Alphonse Gamaldak, president of the Mofu Gudur Inter-Church Committee, said Bible translation reshaped his entire life trajectory. Before receiving any formal education, he learned to read and write in his mother tongue. This linguistic foundation gave him the leeway to master French, eventually leading him to seminary. ‘Yes, the church is awake in Mofu Gudur (a language community of northern Cameroon) because many kids have now grown and seen their lives transformed by the Bible translated into our language,’ he said. The impact extends far beyond the sanctuary. Through mother-tongue functional literacy programmes overseen by the translation project, community members have developed income-generating activities, drastically improving local livelihoods. Today, over 250 literacy teachers are actively instructing inside churches and surrounding villages. Yet, Pastor Gamaldak warned that sustainability requires ongoing investment. ‘There is still much to do,’ he said, ‘like continuing to build the capacity of and support these 250 literacy teachers.’ In 2008, when the Mofu Gudur New Testament was dedicated, the church and the community came together to facilitate the distribution. Five thousand copies were printed, and they were all sold out in the following months. A second run of 4,000 copies was printed. A few years later, it was still hard to obtain a copy. This motivated CABTAL to begin work on the Old Testament, which was dedicated in May 2026. Thanks to the commitment of the local church, the Mofu Gudur people now have a complete Bible. The Takeaway for the Global Alliance For both the African and global audiences at the Yaoundé gathering, panel members underscored a fundamental truth: Bible translation is not an isolated academic exercise. When local churches move from being merely ‘awake’ to being actively engaged, Scripture access unlocks deep spiritual maturity, local resource mobilisation and holistic community development. God alone disarms the hostility of the sinner turning his heart of stone to a heart of flesh (2 Cor 4:4-6). It is God, the Holy Spirit, alone who gives illumination and understanding of His word that we might believe; It is God who raises us from the death of sin, who circumcises the heart; unplugs our ears; It is God alone who can give us a new sense, a spiritual capacity to behold the beauty and unsurpassed excellency of Jesus Christ. The apostle John recorded Jesus saying to Nicodemus that we naturally love darkness, hate the light and WILL NOT come into the light (John 3:19, 20). And since our hardened resistance to God is thus seated in our affections, only God, by His grace, can lovingly change, overcome and pacify our rebellious disposition. The natural man, apart from the quickening work of the Holy Spirit, will not come to Christ on his own since he is at enmity with God and cannot understand spiritual things (1 Cor 2:14). Shining a light into a blind man's eyes will not enable him to see, because eyesight first requires a set of healthy eyes.

In it are opened the fountains of all our regular petitions, and the arguments contained to encourage our hopes for obtaining them. In our addresses to men, our study is to conciliate their favourable audience; but God is most graciously inclined and ready to grant our requests, therefore we are directed to call upon him by the title of ‘Our Father in heaven,’ to assure us of his love and power, and thereby to excite our reverent attention, to raise our affections, to confirm our confidence in prayer. The supreme end of our desires is the glory of God, in conjunction with our own happiness: this is expressed in the two first petitions, that ‘his name may be hallowed,’ and ‘his kingdom come,’ that we may partake of its felicity. In order to this, our desires are directed for the means that are proper and effectual to accomplish it. And those are of two kinds — the good things that conduct us, and the removal of those evils that obstruct our happiness.

featured.content: by Archibald Alexander In ePub , .mobi and .pdf formats On the basis of fifty years as a pastor, preacher and professor at Princeton Theological Seminary, Archibald Alexander (1772-1851) deals with the subjective work of the Holy Spirit in the heart in all its phases, from the new birth until final preparation for heaven. There are two kinds of religious knowledge which, though intimately connected as cause and effect, may nevertheless be distinguished. These are the knowledge of the truth as it is revealed in the Holy Scriptures; and the impression which that truth makes on the human mind when rightly apprehended. The first may be compared to the inscription or image on a seal, the other to the impression made by the seal on the wax. When that impression is clearly and distinctly made, we can understand, by contemplating it, the true inscription on the seal more satisfactorily, than by a direct view of the seal itself. Thus it is found that nothing tends more to confirm and elucidate the truths contained in the Word, than an inward experience of their efficacy on the heart. It cannot, therefore, be uninteresting to the Christian to have these effects, as they consist in the various views and affections of the mind, traced out and exhibited in their connection with the truth, and in their relation to each other.

featured.content: "Although They Knew God ... They Suppressed the Truth..." The opportunities are wide open for Christians to speak with secular people these days, especially if you live in a metropolitan area. The average hipster you may meet in the medium to big sized city is a secularist who may listen to NPR, has a liberal, ecological, and/or anti-capitalist political ideology ... wears vintage clothing from a thrift store and consumes ethically. He or she often either rides a bike, uses public transportation or even may be driving a hybrid or bio-diesel vehicle. This person is deeply concerned with the ethical treatment of animals, is strongly against slavery, torture, racism and political oppression against women. In other words, he takes morality very seriously. Another characteristic of this individual is that he/she thinks Christianity is irrelevant at best. Since we deeply care about the eternal destinies of such individuals how should we go about reaching such a person with the gospel? Where would you start? Once of the more effective ways, I have found, is to remember that that your secular friend already knows God exists. He/she knows God exists and lives as if He does. In Romans chapter 1 Paul clearly teaches this about all people when he says, "For although they knew God" (verse 21) "...by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (verse 18). But how can we demonstrate to your friends that they already believe in God, when intellectually they deny His existence? While there are many ways this could be done, I would like to suggest one way that I have found to be quite persuasive: The knowledge of God through their own morality.

featured.content: On October 31, 1517, Martin Luther, now in his mid-thirties, made his way to the Castle Church in Wittenberg and posted his Ninety-Five Theses on the church door. Originally intended as propositions for public debate, the theses were written in Latin—the language of the scholar, not of the street. Luther could have had no idea that they would echo around Europe and become the catalyst for a spiritual revolution. Many of those who saw the papers on the Castle Church door—which seems to have served as a public notice board—would not have been able to read Latin. But soon the theses were translated into German and thereafter spread throughout Europe like wildfire—indeed, like an “act of God.” What were the Ninety-Five Theses? They were statements aimed directly at specific corruptions in the church of Luther’s day, many of them related to issues of pardon, purgatory, and the power of the pope. The first of them was particularly startling: By saying “Repent,” our Lord and Master Jesus Christ willed that the whole of the life of believers should be repentance. (Dominus et magister noster Iesus Christus dicendo “Poenitentiam agite etc.” omnem vitam fidelium poenitentiam esse voluit.) Luther had grasped that the Vulgate translation of “Repent” ( poenitentiam agite ) was open to the misinterpretation “Do penitence (or penance).” And he had also grasped a principle that John Calvin would later expound with great clarity: penitence or repentance is not the action of a moment; it is the turning around of a life—the rejection of sin effected by the gracious work of the Holy Spirit. It cannot therefore be a single act completed in a moment; it is a style of life that lasts until glory. Luther led a full and adventurous life that only an extensive biography can well describe. He was a remarkable man with enormous God-given energy. His speech was direct and plain and not infrequently earthy. He was a teacher of theology, a preacher of the gospel, and an author of some of the most important books in the Reformation period. Notable among his early publications was his On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church , which exposed the church’s failures, while in On the Freedom of a Christian he explained how in Jesus Christ believers are set free both to love God and to serve their neighbor. Thus he wrote in a beautifully crafted sentence that captures the paradox of the gospel-centered life: “A Christian man is the most free lord of all, and subject to none; a Christian man is the most dutiful servant of all, and subject to everyone.” By his preaching, by writing, and especially by his influence in the explanation of salvation by grace through faith in Christ, Luther was used by God to transform the Christian church. The leading Reformers in England and Scotland were influenced by his writings, often smuggled in by merchant sailors. In Scotland in particular, the martyrs of St. Andrews, Patrick Hamilton and George Wishart (whose bodyguard John Knox had been), were disciples of Luther’s teaching. Likewise in England, the heroic William Tyndale left a legacy not only in his English translation of the Bible but in an entire body of literature that echoed the German Reformer’s work. But what did Luther teach? His chief emphases are aptly summarized in the well-known Reformation solas: (1) sola Scriptura : we come to know God through Scripture alone, not through the traditions of the church as such; (2) sola gratia : we come to receive forgiveness by God’s grace alone, not because we are able to earn merit; (3) sola fide: we receive justification by faith alone, and not by faith plus something else; (4) solus Christus : all of God’s riches are given to us in Christ alone; (5) soli Deo gloria: the goal of all of life is the glory of God alone. These principles simply underlined the emphases Luther found in Scripture. But in context, what is most significant about them is not only what they stressed but what they bypassed. featured.content: “Retirement at last! Now I can sleep as late as I want to. Now I get to do nothing all day.” Such is a popular description of how retirement looks to many people. I know some who would even add, “Now I get to play golf every day.” Obviously, this does not reflect the Christian perspective of someone who understands that his chief end is “to glorify God and enjoy Him forever” (see Westminster Shorter Catechism 1; 1 Cor. 10:31; Rom. 11:36). This is not to say that sleeping later and playing golf are anti-Christian. However, there are some significant ways that retirees can still serve the church. 1. Be a volunteer. Retirees have valuable practical and professional experience that can be used in service to others. For example, some of you may have skill sets and expertise that enable you to erect a building or a cabin at a camp from the ground up in very little time. One organization I’m familiar with travels to camps and other locations, bringing their own living accommodations, tools, and know-how to be a blessing to other ministries. Some may volunteer in maintenance of a church’s lawns and gardens to keep them looking tidy. Volunteers can save churches and various ministries a great deal of money and provide much encouragement to them. The church where I attend has many volunteers (both retired and pre-retired) who help at the annual church youth camps. They serve in the kitchen and dining hall, as cabin staff and counselors, as camp nurses and in technical positions, and pay their own way to camp. While not everyone can serve in such physical ways, everyone can volunteer in some way according to their abilities and gifts: “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another . . . in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:10–11). 2. Show the younger generations a model of an older person who still walks with the Lord. The youth in our churches need models of older believers who are faithful in their daily walk with the Lord. What might this example look like? We can show that we have not waned in faithfulness in our older years, that we are active and unashamed to belong to God’s people, and that we continue to radiate joy in our relationship with the Lord. We can model what it looks like to have no hesitation to speak about Christ in the doctor’s office, store, or when traveling, and that we are not reluctant to share Scripture with other people. Paul wrote to the saints in Philippi: “Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us” (Phil. 3:17). Note these words from the psalmist: O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds. So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation. (Ps. 71:17–18) 3. Regularly attend worship services and wholeheartedly participate. Not only should retirees maintain a faithful walk with the Lord, but they ought to remain consistent in their attendance at the regular worship services of the church. It is a testament to the Lord’s faithfulness when they are seen in the pews, not just taking up space or putting in their time, but wholeheartedly and enthusiastically singing, listening, and note-taking. This is important because it seems that many young people today view church as optional rather than a joyful habit. Granted, this should begin with the influence of godly parents, but it is reinforced and aided when the testimony of the older generation displays undiminished love for corporate worship, viewing it not as drudgery but delight. Hebrews 10:23–25 instructs us in this way: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful. And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near. 4. featured.title_zh: 这五个唯独对今天的教会仍然重要吗？
featured.content: The five solas (Latin for “alone”) of the Reformation—Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, to the glory of God alone—are indispensable for the church in any era. They will always be relevant because they summarize the biblical gospel, which is the church’s lifeblood in every age. They are particularly significant today because even professing evangelicals, to say nothing of the culture around us, are being tempted to abandon the gospel. Therefore, the church must recognize the dire need of not only defending the five solas but also celebrating them. The five solas are important for us today for at least three reasons. 1. The five solas set apart the true gospel from every other religion, worldview, or philosophy. Every day, the world calls out its siren song of spiritual compromise. Satan loves to negotiate the nonnegotiables of biblical truth. He whispers the lie that we don’t need to have strong convictions about the Bible as our only standard of truth or hold firm to the teaching that only those who trust Christ alone for salvation are right with God. The temptation to downplay doctrine is unceasing. A winsome but unyielding grasp of the five solas can help us resist these attractive lies. 2. The five solas provide us with unspeakable comfort in a chaotic world. The pace of modern life is unsustainable. It colors our understanding of “the normal Christian life.” We tend to equate busyness in ministry with productiveness for Jesus. But the two must not be confused. Knowing that we are saved by God’s grace alone through faith alone gives us rest from an exhausting world. We leave behind a performance mindset in our relationship with God and embrace a life of trusting, resting grace. Safe in the arms of our Savior, we are set free to let go of trying to earn what God freely gives us—Christ Himself. 3. The five solas remind us that our salvation is secure. Only when we are assured of the love of God will we live out the commands of God. The five solas enable us to say with David, “Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day” (Ps. 119:97). Following Jesus, obeying Him by the Spirit, and killing sin become our joy. So many Christians drift, unconsciously most of the time, to the belief that God loves them when they obey. But the true gospel of the five solas pulls us back to the bedrock scriptural truth that God loves us and therefore we obey. The difference is subtle, but it makes all the difference in our daily lives. Your Father loves you! He is pleased with you in Christ. When those realities come home, John’s words become our delightful creed: “For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). In sum, nothing is more urgent for the church than protecting, propagating, and passing on the true gospel encapsulated by the five solas . It is our only hope, our greatest comfort, and our supreme joy. Most of all, these biblical teachings will always be important because they bring us to Christ, who is our life. 1 Footnotes Editor's Note: This article was originally published January 19, 2022. ↩

featured.content: In the old city of Geneva, Switzerland, there is a large park on the grounds of the University of Geneva that commemorates the Reformation. That park is adorned with a huge wall, called the International Monument to the Reformation or simply the Reformation Wall. In statues and bas-reliefs, the wall depicts figures from the Reformation including John Calvin, John Knox, William Farel, and Theodore Beza. Surrounding these and other statues, the motto of the Reformation is inscribed on each side: post tenebras lux —after darkness, light. This phrase refers not only to the unveiling and liberation of the Scriptures—which were made available to the common people during the Reformation—but also to the loss and recovery of the most important biblical doctrine there is: the doctrine of justification by faith alone. This was the primary and central issue of the Protestant Reformation. During the dispute between the Protestants and the Roman Catholics, both sides saw that justification was so important that no compromise was possible. Both sides were convinced that what was at stake in the doctrine of justification was the very essence of the biblical gospel. When the gospel is at stake, everything is at stake, because the gospel tells us how we can be right with God. In Galatians 1:6–9, Paul writes about the importance of getting the gospel right: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ. But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed. This Apostle was a man who was constantly extolling the virtues of patience, gentleness, meekness, charity, and tolerance; who, conversely, constantly rebuked the sins of contentiousness, divisiveness, quarrelsome spirits, belligerence, and so on. This man said that we ought to strive as much as we possibly can to live at peace with all men; he was known as the Apostle of peace and unity. Yet suddenly he came to a point over a doctrine where he said, “There can be no toleration here. To tolerate the distortion of the gospel into another gospel is to tolerate the intolerable.” The first thing that Paul did was express his amazement—not that the people had left the gospel that he had preached to them, but that they had done it so quickly. He was hardly gone from their midst before they wanted to listen to the teachings of the Judaizers, who insisted that one cannot be saved by faith in Christ alone but must also have good works and obedience to the law in order to be saved. This “other gospel” was no gospel at all—there is only one gospel, the gospel of God, revealed in and through Christ and proclaimed and expounded by the Apostles. The stakes are so high when it comes to this point that Paul pronounced a curse on anyone who teaches otherwise. The Greek work translated “accursed” is anathema —damned. The Apostle understood that the issue of justification was no mere academic issue, but one that touches every person’s life ultimately. It can be summed up in one question: How are we saved? It is a life-and-death matter, an eternal life matter. The New Testament makes it clear that each of us will be called into account before God, and that God is righteous while we’re not. The doctrine of justification addresses the solution to that problem, declaring how we, as unjust people, can be reconciled to a just and holy God. So if there’s anything in the essence of the Christian faith, of the good news of the gospel, it’s this doctrine. featured.title_zh: 西奥多·贝扎是谁？
featured.content: Theodore Beza is an unfamiliar figure today in the evangelical world. He has been much maligned by many historians and theologians who created the image of an austere man who turned Calvin’s theology into an arid scholastic system. This image is actually very far from the truth. So who was Theodore Beza really? He was born in Vézelay, France, in 1519 in an affluent family of the minor French nobility. His life spanned almost the whole sixteenth century, and he died in 1605 at the age of eighty-six. By God’s providence, there were two clear turning points in his life. The first occurred at the age of nine when he was placed as a lodger with a Lutheran scholar, Melchior Wolmar, who became his preceptor. He spent seven years with Wolmar, who taught him law, Latin, and Greek. Interestingly, one of Wolmar’s other students during that time was none other than Calvin, who was just ten years older than Beza. Wolmar gave Beza a first-rate education, and, like Calvin, Beza was likely more fluent in Latin than in French. More importantly, Wolmar was instrumental in his journey toward the new Reformed faith. It was through Wolmar that, sometime around 1535, Beza read a book by the Swiss Reformer Heinrich Bullinger and was converted. Years later, Beza wrote to Bullinger: “You made known to me true piety, and its purest source: The Word of God.” 1 However, Beza had a lot to lose if he disclosed his newfound faith. He received substantial ecclesiastical incomes through one of his uncles, who was an abbot, and this allowed him to enjoy a life of pleasure in Paris, dedicating himself to poetry and humanistic studies. For several years, he kept his faith secret, and he secretly married Claudine Denosse, the daughter of a Parisian Protestant merchant. Beza promised he would marry her publicly whenever they could find a truly Reformed church. The second turning point of his life came in 1548 when he contracted the plague and came close to death. He took it as a clear warning from God and came out openly about his faith. Shortly after, he fled to Geneva. Theodore and Claudine were publicly married by Calvin himself, and they remained devoted to each other and to the cause of Christ until Claudine’s death in 1588. After teaching Greek in Lausanne for a few years, Beza settled in Geneva permanently in 1558, mainly because of his admiration for Calvin. He lived there until his death, faithfully serving alongside Calvin and assuming his mantle as leader of the French Reformed church after Calvin’s death in 1564. Beza’s legacy is immense and multifaceted, and it is difficult to summarize it in a few words. He was first and foremost a man of letters. One of his first tasks in Geneva was to complete the translation of the Psalms from Hebrew into French for the Huguenot psalter, a translation left unfinished by another Reformed poet at his death. Beza also published a critical edition of the Greek New Testament that was influential on the Textus Receptus, from which the King James Bible was translated. In fact, the 1565 edition was dedicated to Queen Elizabeth I. In many ways, this was Beza’s lifetime project. He tirelessly corrected and improved the text and published several editions, with the last major revision appearing in 1598. In 1559, he published a “Confession of the Christian Faith,” addressed to his father, to explain why he had embraced the Reformed faith. Although it was penned in a few days, it was hugely popular, as it was published at least thirty-five times during his lifetime and translated into Latin, English, German, and Dutch. He consolidated Calvin’s legacy in Geneva by preaching regularly and teaching theology for forty years. We know from several sources that his teaching was greatly appreciated. For example, an alumnus wrote in 1578: We listened to you with so much admiration and pleasure. featured.title_zh: 新教改革的原因是什么？
featured.content: What was the matter with the Protestant Reformation? It might seem like a strange question. Some might say that there was nothing the matter with the Reformation, that it was the acme of spiritual recovery of biblical Christianity in church history and therefore was a sort of golden age of biblical faith. Others might say that the matter with the Reformation was that there was one at all, since it produced the largest schism in church history. That’s not what I mean, however, when I ask about what was the matter with the Protestant Reformation. I’m not using the word matter in the normal way, which typically indicates that something is wrong. When we ask, “What’s the matter with you?” we are assuming that something is wrong or that we’re looking for fault. What I mean, by contrast, is this: What was the essence, the substance, or what is called in philosophy the material cause of the Protestant Reformation? Another way to ask it would be this: What was the chief issue that provoked such massive consequences as this split that occurred in the sixteenth century? When historians consider the causes of the Protestant Reformation, they often use distinctions originally set forth by the philosopher Aristotle, and they distinguish between the formal cause and the material cause . The formal cause, the intellectual background to the issue, was a dispute over the seat of final authority that binds the Christian conscience. We’ll look at that under the heading of sola Scriptura . The material cause , however, the substantive issue that was the core point of dispute, was the doctrine of justification. The Protestant view of this matter is expressed in the shorthand of the Latin phrase sola fide . This is the first of the Latin slogans of the Reformation known as the five solas . They are sola fide , justification is by faith alone; sola gratia , salvation is by grace alone; solus Christus , salvation is through Christ alone; sola Scriptura , the sole authority that binds the conscience of the Christian is the Bible alone; and then, finally, soli Deo gloria , to God alone belongs the glory. Sola fide is shorthand for the central issue of the Reformation, the material cause, which was the question of justification. The Protestant Reformers set forth a doctrine that our justification is by faith and by faith alone without any mixture of good works or merit on our part. To understand sola fide in its historical context, we have to understand something about the theological dispute based on the Roman Catholic understanding of justification. At the heart of this dispute was not a tangential debate over how many angels can dance on the head of a pin or a needless controversy over pedantic points of theology that only academics care about. Rather, this issue touched the very heart of the Christian faith because the question of justification is designed to answer this deeper question: How can an unjust person possibly survive the judgment of a just and holy God? In our day, the doctrine of justification has been degraded in terms of its perceived importance. Historically, the differences among churches over how we obtain a right standing before God were considered significant; those differences have now been minimized as having no great weight. We’re living in a time of relativism, which says that there is no objective truth, and pluralism, which declares that there are many different approaches to truth and views of truth. Therefore, people assert, doctrinal issues should never divide us because what really counts are personal relationships, not doctrine. That notion is propounded even though the New Testament is replete with Apostolic concern about correct doctrine. Sadly, that’s not where the church is in this day and age, and sometimes we have to ask, Why? Some people are in church Sunday after Sunday, are continually exposed to the preaching of the gospel, and are members of the church but have never really committed their lives to Christ. S

featured.title_zh: 男人为教会服务的5种方式
featured.content:
Pastors are often asked about how to encourage men to be more involved in the life of the church. For a variety of reasons, the perception among men is that the church is not a place for doing manly things. Unless men take active leadership roles, the involvement of men in the church is often limited to attending a single service on Sunday. The absence of male service in the church is detrimental to the progress and health of the entire body. Perhaps the proverbial question, “Adam, where are you?” continues to be asked most often regarding men serving in the kingdom of God.
There appears to be a significant disconnect for men between certain activities that provide a sense of purpose and accomplishment—such as work, sports, and other recreational activities—and active service the church. Great encouragement is needed for men to view serving in the church as a critical component of their calling in this life. Such service is not merely personally fulfilling, but it builds up and strengthens the entire body of Christ. There is nothing more Christlike than a man laying down his life for his friends. This, according to Jesus, is true greatness.
There are many ways to encourage men to serve in the church. Sometimes, however, we think too highly about this question. It’s always important to begin with those things that seem insignificant to us. One does not have to be an ordained office bearer to do great works among us. In a word: Think smaller. It is in the little things that great things are achieved, even if it is taking a cup of cold water to someone in need. With these things in mind, what follows are five simple encouragements for men regarding how they might serve well in the local church.
1. Pursue growth in the Scriptures.
First and most important is the personal growth of the man himself. A great servant is not created by merely doing. It begins with the mind and the heart. A servant is formed, not coerced by guilt. The mind must be renewed by understanding the love of Christ for us, then our love for others becomes properly motivated. Becoming a servant happens by pursuing growth in the Scriptures. Yes, this requires heartfelt attendance to the means of grace in worship on Sunday. This is a top priority. But it also requires the weekly pursuit of our own development spiritually toward the end of helping others grow in the faith. Active involvement in Bible studies and other groups centered around the Word and prayer will help shape us to have the mind of Christ. Growing together with other men in study is an equipping type of service in the body that will result in cultivating fellowship, making us effective in serving the needs of others. Make use of these opportunities for growth.
2. Pursue the qualities of an office bearer.
Most men reading this article may feel unequipped or uncalled to ordained service in the church. The result is that men think they do not have the gifts for this high calling and so service in the body is often left to ordained men. This is certainly a wrong view of the basic calling of the Christian man. While the requirements for office bearers are described in passages such as 1 Timothy 3, this does not mean that these qualities should only be pursued by ordained men. All men should think about the use of these gifts even if they do not serve in an official capacity. In general, men ought to aspire to practice them. Opportunities abound such as reading the Scriptures to encourage the afflicted, visiting the sick, helping those in need, and praying for the body. Recognizing that these duties belong to all men is an important first step, then knowing the body and serving them is what follows.
3. Help the widow and orphan.
